TITLE: BLACK WOMEN'S LIT RENAISSANCE
COMMENTS: Open to First Years and Sophomores only.
Course Description: The twenty-year period between 1970 and 1990 is often referred to as the “Black Women’s Literary Renaissance” due to the unprecedented amount of literary and cultural production from black women in the United States. This course explores its profound contributions to black life and literature. Students will examine the intersections and oppositions among political movements, such as the Lesbian Feminist Movement and the Black Power Movement, and identify how these connections shaped the aesthetic landscape of the time. Course materials will include essays, novels, poems, and visual art, featuring Alice Walker, Toni Cade Bambara, bell hooks, Lorna Simpson, and others.

TITLE: ELEMENTARY JAZZ DANCE
Course Description: An introductory technique course exploring jazz dance as a form grounded in Black American cultural and performance traditions. Students develop foundational skills in rhythm, coordination, and jazz vocabulary while situating studio practice within the historical evolution of jazz dance. Attention is given to stylistic nuance, musicality, and expressive range within jazz movement. Open to all students; no previous dance experience required.

TITLE: DIVERSITY RECONSIDERED
Course Description: An examination of the emergence of Africana Studies as a transdisciplinary field of social and cultural critique and politics. Explores the work of foundational (e.g., W.E.B Dubois and Anna Julia Cooper) and contemporary figures. Topics include but are not limited to the history of Africana thought, race and global racial formation, resistance and politics, intersectionality, gender and sexuality, representation, white privilege, belonging, Blackness, and diaspora.
Prerequisite Narrative: AFRST-102, AFRST-112, AFRST-130, AFRST-190 or permission of the instructor

TITLE: GENDER,SPACE,IDENTITY
Course Name: Gender, Space and Identity in the African Diaspora
COMMENTS: Open to Sr, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: This course examines how racialized and gendered identities are made in relation to space. How does gender intersect with race, class and other power relations embedded in the places we live? How do women and men come to occupy different places in the world – literally and figuratively – or occupy the same places in different ways? Case studies focus on identity making in relation to the body and the course more broadly focuses on the intersection of race, class, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity as matrices of social and structural power relations and hierarchies.

TITLE: TONI MORRISON
Course Description: This course is an in-depth study of Toni Morrison’s fictional works and critical writing. Students will explore her creative and scholarly contributions to ideas of community and genealogy, as well as to representations of race, gender, and nation. Students will also explore her attention to language, form, and literary theory. In studying both Morrison’s formal and theoretical commitments, students will develop an awareness of how literature serves as a vehicle for animating and critiquing social, historical, and ethical concerns in our world. Assignments will include short critical essays, collaborative presentations and projects, and readings will include "The Source of Self-Regard," "The Bluest Eye," "Song of Solomon," and "Jazz."

TITLE: THE BLACK SELF
Course Name: The Black Self: Identity and Consciousness
Course Description: A philosophical exploration of a variety of historical and contemporary works that illuminate and influence the phenomenological experience of being black.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in philosophy or Africana studies, or consent of instructor

TITLE: JAZZ CONNECTIONS
Course Description: An advanced jazz course that builds on the topics covered in Jazz Foundations (MUSIC 161), and examines the construction of the “jazz tradition” from a historiographical perspective. Considers how the development of jazz, and its construction in the context of educational institutions, both reflects and shapes concepts of race and gender in American culture. Includes an examination of the impact of jazz genres including hip hop, R&B, and gospel, and focuses on the international proliferation of jazz.
Prerequisite Narrative: MUSIC 161/261, AFRST 161/261, MUSIC 257/357, AFRST 257/357, or consent instructor
Notes: Not open to students who have taken MUSIC/AFRST 259/359. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor's permission.

TITLE: URBAN WORLDS
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores.
Course Description: Since the great northern migrations of the World War II era much of African American experience has been lived out in urban worlds, from New York to San Francisco. The city has held out a peculiar hope for a better life, celebrated in fiction, scholarly literature and popular culture, since the Black exodus from the South. We explore the American story of promise and inclusion and the visible and at times hidden workings of exclusion, two stories that unfold simultaneously in the experience of urban America.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Africana Studies or consent of instructor

TITLE: JAZZ CONNECTIONS
COMMENTS: Instructor's signature required.
Course Description: An advanced jazz course that builds on the topics covered in Jazz Foundations (MUSIC 161), and examines the construction of the “jazz tradition” from a historiographical perspective. Considers how the development of jazz, and its construction in the context of educational institutions, both reflects and shapes concepts of race and gender in American culture. Includes an examination of the impact of jazz genres including hip hop, R&B, and gospel, and focuses on the international proliferation of jazz.
Prerequisite Narrative: MUSIC 161/261, AFRST 161/261, MUSIC 257/357, AFRST 257/357, or consent instructor
Notes: Not open to students who have taken MUSIC/AFRST 259/359. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor's permission.

TITLE: SEM BLACK FEMINIST THOUGHT
Course Description: Interdisciplinary examination of the tradition of black feminist thought as it spans African and African-American heritages. Exploration of how black women are not simply victims of oppression but visionary agents of change. Areas examined include history, literature,music,art,education, sociology and film. There is intersectional analysis of the social, structural, and institutional hierarchies within the identities of women of African descent (gender/transgender, race, white supremacy, sexual/affectional orientation, class, color, and ability).
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Women's and Gender Studies or consent of instructor

TITLE: INDIGENOUS ORAL TRADITIONS
Course Description: This course examines various elements of Indigenous oral traditions, including oral literatures like creation stories, narratives, cautionary tales, formal oratory, dance, and song, theorizing how some of these oral traditions can also be considered forms of writing. We will study different Indigenous methods of performance, analyzing elements such as tone and pitch, gestures, silence, back-channeling, turn-taking, taking of floor, and traditional openings and closings. We will also compare conversational norms, metaphors, puns, and humor used in diverse Indigenous cultures. Finally, we will examine the goals of decolonization in many Indigenous communities and explore the practices and discourses intended to decolonize and/or Indigenize daily life and promote Indigenous identities in the coming generations.

TITLE: SIBERIAN TEXT
Course Description: This course is an exploration of five centuries of writing in and about Siberia. While we will root ourselves in the socio-historical context, our main goal is to engage meaningfully with the very process of the formation of the Siberian Text. By this, scholars of the region mean the body of works that emerged out of the geographical, political, anthropological, and cultural categorizations of Siberia. The plurality of voices and the diversity of spatial experiences engaged in the process of creating the Siberian Text include travelers, criminals, political prisoners, religious dissenters, shamans, hunters, ethnographers, missionaries, vagabonds, and peasants. Probing the fraught legacy of the current spatial discourse on Siberia, the course will examine a variety of media and genres, including official documents, travelogues, oral tradition(s), works of fiction, autobiographies, pictorial art, and film. In addition to the transnational and transhistorical dimensions, we will engage with theories of space and place, imagined geographies, and ecocriticism.

TITLE: EMERGENT INDIGENEITY
Course Name: Where Tradition Meets Modernity: Emergent Indigeneity
COMMENTS: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab.
Course Description: This class will explore Emergent Indigeneity: how Indigenous identity is a dynamic and continually evolving process of redefining and making that rejects fixed notions of “purity” or “authenticity.” We will look at the ways modern American Indian and First Nations artists draw upon traditional practices, materials, and cosmologies within their tribally-specific knowledge systems, but use modern technologies, methods, and materials to communicate what it means to be Indigenous in the late 20th and early 21st century. For example, we might look at how Native writers redefine a literary genre drawing on specific Indigenous knowledge systems, how some Indigenous pop-music artists sample traditional songs, or how TV writers represent cultural practices in a modern context. Will include literature, film, TV, music, social media, and material culture, as well as beadwork, performance art, and modern art.

TITLE: INTRO TO NATIVE AMER STUDIES
Course Description: The course serves as an introduction to the interdisciplinary field of Native American Studies, exploring both the complexity and diversity of Native American experiences. Students learn about both historical and contemporary events and issues from Indigenous perspectives and develop new ways of thinking and talking about - and with - Native Americans.

TITLE: ROOTS TO COUNTRY MUSIC
Course Name: Roots Music to Country Music: The Making of an American Sound
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Study of country music from its roots in cowboy songs, fiddle tunes, blues, bluegrass, and gospel hymns to current artists like The [Dixie] Chicks, Taylor Swift, and Brad Paisley. Artists include the Carter Family, Hank Williams, Patsy Cline, Dolly Parton, Willie Nelson, Emmylou Harris, Lynyrd Skynyrd, & Garth Brooks. Study of the musical elements, social class, gender roles, and cultural contexts of styles such as Western Swing, Honky-Tonk, Rockabilly, the Nashville Sound, Southern Rock, and Alt-country. Includes films such as Coal Miner's Daughter, Nashville, and O Brother, Where Art Thou?
Notes: No previous knowledge of music required. Music concentrators and minors are strongly encouraged to register for MUSIC-217. MUSIC-217 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 200-level only with instructor’s permission.

TITLE: ROOTS TO COUNTRY MUSIC
Course Name: Roots Music to Country Music: The Making of an American Sound
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, and 1st Yrs. Open to Music majors/minors only or instructor permission.
Course Description: Study of country music from its roots in cowboy songs, fiddle tunes, blues, bluegrass, and gospel hymns to current artists like The [Dixie] Chicks, Taylor Swift, and Brad Paisley. Artists include the Carter Family, Hank Williams, Patsy Cline, Dolly Parton, Willie Nelson, Emmylou Harris, Lynyrd Skynyrd, & Garth Brooks. Study of the musical elements, social class, gender roles, and cultural contexts of styles such as Western Swing, Honky-Tonk, Rockabilly, the Nashville Sound, Southern Rock, and Alt-country. Includes films such as Coal Miner's Daughter, Nashville, and O Brother, Where Art Thou?
Notes: No previous knowledge of music required. Music concentrators and minors are strongly encouraged to register for MUSIC-217. MUSIC-217 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 200-level only with instructor’s permission.

TITLE: NATIVE AMER RELIGIOUS FREEDOM
Course Description: Is American religious freedom a reality, an unfinished project, or merely a myth? This course explores how Native Americans have struggled for religious freedom in the United States, focusing on contemporary legal battles to protect sacred lands, repatriate ancestral remains and objects, and defend the ceremonial consumption of peyote.

TITLE: MUSIC IN AMER FILM
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Years.
Course Description: Examination of music in American film from silent films to the present with emphasis on the golden age of Hollywood. Topics include the development of musical conventions in film, different approaches of film composers (Steiner, Tiomkin, Rózsa, Herrmann, Newman, Bernstein, Williams), the meanings that music brings to film narratives. Includes films such as Casablanca, The Adventures of Robin Hood, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, A Streetcar Named Desire, Amadeus, The Shawshank Redemption, Oh Brother, Where Art Thou? Special attention to Hitchcock films (Psycho, Vertigo, Rear Window).
Prerequisite Narrative: Two courses in Music, Cinema and Media Studies, or Literature
Notes: Three hours per week for film viewings in addition to class time. Music 345 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor’s permission.

TITLE: SEM: INDIGENOUS ECOLOGIES
Course Description: This interdisciplinary seminar explores the traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) of indigenous peoples. Drawing upon scholarship from such diverse fields as acoustic ecology, ethno-ecology, ethnography, geography, environmental history, Native American and Indigenous Studies, and religious studies, we will examine indigenous knowledge about particular species and relationships between them.

TITLE: MUSIC IN AMER FILM
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Sophomores, & 1st Yrs. Open to Music majors/minors only or instructor permission required.
Course Description: Examination of music in American film from silent films to the present with emphasis on the golden age of Hollywood. Topics include the development of musical conventions in film, different approaches of film composers (Steiner, Tiomkin, Rózsa, Herrmann, Newman, Bernstein, Williams), the meanings that music brings to film narratives. Includes films such as Casablanca, The Adventures of Robin Hood, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, A Streetcar Named Desire, Amadeus, The Shawshank Redemption, Oh Brother, Where Art Thou? Special attention to Hitchcock films (Psycho, Vertigo, Rear Window).
Prerequisite Narrative: Two courses in Music, Cinema and Media Studies, or Literature
Notes: Three hours per week for film viewings in addition to class time. Music 345 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor’s permission.

TITLE: PRIN SOC & CULTURAL ANTHR
Course Name: Principles of Social and Cultural Anthropology
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: Cross-cultural approaches to the study of such topics as inequality, polity, language, economic behavior, the body, and other categorical distinctions emergent from human practice.  Exposure to anthropological theory, methods, and ethnography.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: DIGITAL TECH&SOC TRAN
COMMENTS: Open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
Course Description: Examines some of the ways in which digital technologies have been imagined to be important to social change, transformation, or innovation.  Proponents of the use of digital technologies toward social change have focused on their speed, connectivity, and capacity.  The course will introduce some of these arguments, will review some critiques of these arguments, and will suggest – via ethnographic cases – that digital technologies, like all sociocultural forms, should be studied with careful attention to contextual concerns.
Prerequisite Narrative: One 100-level course in Anthropology or consent of instructor.

TITLE: MEDICAL ANTHROPOLOGY
Course Name: Medical Anthropology: Objects, Subjects, and Narratives
Course Description: Medicine does more than diagnose and treat illness. It produces knowledge about bodies, shapes understandings of health and disease, and influences how individuals experience themselves and others. This course examines medicine as a social, cultural, and political practice through three interconnected themes: objects, subjects, and narratives. Drawing on ethnographic research and critical social theory, we explore how medical knowledge is produced, how bodies become objects of scientific inquiry and intervention, and how medical categories and institutions shape identities, experiences, and social relations. We consider the material worlds of medicine, from pharmaceuticals and medical technologies to the human body itself; the formation of medical subjects through diagnosis, treatment, and care; and the narratives through which illness, suffering, and healing acquire meaning.
Notes: Engaging with questions of power, knowledge, embodiment, and inequality, students will examine topics including medicalization, mental health, pharmaceuticalization, biological citizenship, structural violence, and the politics of life and death. Throughout the course, we ask how medicine both reflects and transforms the societies in which it operates.

TITLE: THE CORPORATION
Course Description: The Corporation examines how corporations have evolved as economic, political, and cultural institutions, shaping and reflecting the societies in which they operate. Drawing on historical analysis and ethnographic perspectives, the course traces their development from early chartered companies to the 2008 financial crisis, exploring key transformations in corporate structure, legal personhood, and financialization. We will consider how corporations have been shaped by historical forces such as colonialism, industrialization, and neoliberalism, while also analyzing their cultural logics, organizational practices, and symbolic power. Readings will examine how corporations have reshaped labor, culture, and economic inequality, as well as the ways they have been challenged and reformed. By examining corporate influence across time and space, students will gain a deeper understanding of its role in the modern world.

TITLE: AUDIOVISUAL ENTERTAINMENT
Course Description: This course explores how narratives and identities are constructed, mediated, and consumed through a combination of sound and image in audiovisual entertainment such as anime, cartoons, and video games. Drawing on anthropology, media studies, performance studies, and sociolinguistics, we will explore audiovisual entertainment not merely as a leisure consumption but as the means through which creative workers and fan-viewers co-operatively construe and (re)imagine social relations.

TITLE: ANTHROPOLOGY OF PLAY
Course Name: Anthropology of Play: Toys and the Politics of Playfulness
Course Description: This course examines play as a serious social, cultural, and political practice. Drawing on anthropological theories of ritual, performance, materiality, affect, and infrastructure, we explore how play organizes social life across contexts, from children’s games and sports to toys, anime, video games, trading cards, and digital platforms. Rather than treating play as trivial or escapist, the course approaches it as a domain through which identities are formed, communities are sustained, economies are structured, and power is negotiated.

TITLE: HISTORY OF IDEAS
Course Description: A consideration of major paradigms in anthropology from the 19th century to the present. The influence of various theoretical perspectives on ethnographic and archaeological description and analysis.

TITLE: SOCIOLINGUISTICS GLOBALIZTN
Course Description: Explores the relationship between language variation and change, on the one hand, and the movement of sound and image in the wake of social and political economic processes variously identified as globalization, on the other hand.  Of special concern are the ways in which processes of globalization are mediated by institutional and national forms.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Anthropology or consent of instructor

TITLE: FOOD JUSTICE MOHAWK VALLEY
Course Name: Food Justice in the Mohawk Valley
Course Description: Students will grapple with the inherent tension between the fact that there are people who live in the area that don’t have enough to eat and the way that all attempts to mitigate social problems are inevitably informed by certain kinds of cultural/economic/political conceptual frameworks that often remain unexamined and/or invisible. As we work our way through the course readings, the students will be asked to pair up with a local organization that is working to alleviate food-related problems in the area. As they work with the organizations, the students will be tasked with examining the successes of, and the difficulties faced by, the institutions, including the ways that people complicate any implementation of a solution.
Prerequisite Narrative: ANTHR-113 or by permission of instructor

TITLE: SR THESIS CULTURAL ANTHR
Course Name: Senior Thesis Project in Cultural Anthropology
Course Description: The research process as it relates to the fulfillment of the senior project, including the revision of the draft created during the senior seminar and extension of cultural analysis.  Honors in the concentration partly depends on an A- or higher in the course.

TITLE: SECOND TERM ARABIC
Course Description: Continued study with emphasis on verbal proficiency, reading and listening comprehension. Highly interactive with supplemental Language Center projects and activities.

TITLE: MINORITIES IN THE MIDDLE EAST
Course Name: Minorities in the Middle East: History, Religion, and Relations with Political Powers
Course Description: This course explores how minority communities in the Middle East—Druze, ʿAlawites, Kurds, Yezidis, Armenians, Maronites, Copts, Assyrians, and others—have been formed and transformed from the late Ottoman era to the present. Beginning with the shift from imperial pluralism to nation-state “minorities,” it examines how religion, identity, nationalism, and political power shape communal identity and minority–state relations. Case studies span Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, addressing genocide, displacement, nationalism, citizenship, security, and diaspora. Drawing on history, anthropology, religious studies, and political science, students examine how communities negotiate identity, power, and recognition in a plural Middle East. This course examines historical and contemporary experiences of minority communities in the Middle East. Some course materials address difficult subjects, including genocide, mass violence, persecution, forced displacement, sexual violence, religious and ethnic discrimination, and war. These topics are approached in their historical and scholarly contexts and are essential to understanding the experiences of the communities studied in the course.

TITLE: FOURTH TERM ARABIC
Course Description: Advanced level study with emphasis on verbal proficiency, reading and listening comprehension. Highly interactive with supplemental Language Center projects and activities. Short readings from authentic sources.
Prerequisite Narrative: ARABC-115, ARABC-116, and ARABC-215 or placement

TITLE: ADVANCED ARABIC
Course Description: Advanced Arabic is a course designed for students who have completed four semesters of Arabic. The course will help students move from Intermediate Middle level to Advanced. Students will focus on acquiring more vocabulary and more knowledge of the fundamental grammatical and morphological structures of the language. They will also learn about the literary traditions of the Arab World through readings of abridged literary works. The instructor will select the literary work and prepare all the material used for the class.
Prerequisite Narrative: ARABC-115, ARABC-116, ARABC-215, and ARABC-216 or consent of instructor
Notes: This course is sponsored by the New York Six Liberal Arts Consortium, from an award by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation.

TITLE: PRINCIPLES OF ARCHAEOLOGY
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: An introduction to the fundamentals of archaeology, with emphasis on human biological and cultural records. Topics include a review of archaeological field methods such as sampling, survey and excavation, and analytic methods such as dating, typology and formation processes. Three hours of class with lab exercises embedded within that time.
Notes: Occasionally two sections of this course are offered.

TITLE: ARCHAEOLOGY OF DEATH
Course Description: While death is a human universal, the ways societies deal with death, bodies, and burial vary greatly. This course explores mortuary practices through the archaeological record and what they can tell us about ritual, social, economic, and ideological institutions in the past.

TITLE: NORTH AMERICAN ARCHAEOLOGY
Course Description: The history of Native American cultural development prior to European contact.Topics include the timing and effects of human entry into North America, ice-age adaptations, plant and animal domestication, agriculture and beginnings of complex societies. This course will also consider the contemporary debates archaeologists grapple with when interpreting the region’s deeper history.

TITLE: ARCHAEOLOGY OF WATER
Course Description: Water is many things at once: a basic biological necessity, a sacred substance, and a source of political power. Today, water crises reshape lives around the world, from droughts and vanishing aquifers in North America and West Asia to the rising coastlines threatening communities in the Gulf Coast and Southeast Asia. This course examines multiple themes on water through archaeological and anthropological case studies, approaches, and concepts. We'll look at how humans have exploited, managed, and made meaning out of water for the last several millennia, from the earliest farming and herding societies to current concerns on climate and AI infrastructure.

TITLE: CRAFTING CULTURE
Course Name: Crafting Culture: How Artisans Shape Society
Course Description: How can crafting shape societies? This course examines how crafting is not only the production of handmade goods but also a deeply social practice embedded within geological landscapes, belief systems, and political economies. Drawing on key concepts in archaeology, anthropology, Indigenous studies, art history, and museum studies, students will analyze archaeological and ethnographic case studies on crafting practices (e.g., pottery production, textile weaving, beadwork) across various cultural contexts.

TITLE: SR THESIS ARCHAEOLOGY
Course Description: Continuation of participation in ARCH-551 with revision and expansion of the senior thesis.  Honors in the concentration is partly dependent on an A- or better in the course.

TITLE: DRAWING
Course Description: This course will introduce drawing as both a tool for generating ideas, and as an art form in itself. Classes will feature experiments designed to spark and sustain creative impulses, as well as more traditional drawing exercises to train the eye and hand. This will be a multidisciplinary approach, focusing less on perfecting a craft than on building communication skills through visual language. Through discussion and critique, students will develop critical skills and learn how to convey their concepts with simple mark-making.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: INTRODUCTION TO CERAMICS
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph, and Juniors.
Course Description: Handbuilding techniques will be employed to explore the sculptural possibilities of clay. A developed visual and conceptual vocabulary will accompany the technical aspects of ceramics through studio practice and class critique.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: ART & THE ENVIRONMENT
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph, & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Three-dimensional explorations will focus and reflect upon our relationship with the natural and constructed world. Emphasis on process and the language of materials will direct form, meaning, and the context of objects and installations created. A developed visual and conceptual vocabulary will accompany studio practice and class critique.

TITLE: INTRODUCTION TO SCULPTURE
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: This course will provide extensive opportunities to develop observational, conceptual and technical skills in sculpture. Basic woodworking, assemblage, casting, carving and installation methods will be covered, while examining the unique demands and benefits of working in three-dimensions. Through lectures, discussions and critiques, students will delve deeply into what it means to make sculpture in the 21st century.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: INTRO TO MEDIA:INTEGRATED MED
Course Name: Introduction to Media: Integrated Media and Emerging Practices
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph, Jrs, and Srs.
Course Description: This course will serve as an introduction to digital technology in contemporary art making as it relates to interactivity, collaboration, and emerging practices.  Emphasis will be placed on hands on experimentation and exploration across disciplines. We will cover installation art, web art, digital and time-based art, and immersive environments. Students will gain an overview of emerging digital practices, collaborative production strategies and correlations to social, aesthetic and theoretical issues. Other topics may include virtuality, performance, cyborgs, and network culture.

TITLE: INTRO TO PHOTOGRAPHY
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs., Soph, & Juniors.
Course Description: Fundamentals of photography through the use of both analog and digital SLR cameras, black and white darkroom techniques, film scanning and digital printing.  Emphasis on development of technical and aesthetic skills, and the potential of the medium as a tool for artistic expression.  Cameras will be provided by the College.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: FIGURE DRAWING
Course Description: Application of basic drawing principles to the representation of the human figure, with emphasis on anatomy and proportion. Examination of related topics such as the figure in the environment and portraiture.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: INTRODUCTION TO PAINTING
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph., and Jrs. Only.
Course Description: Introduction to the study of the methods and techniques of oil painting, with emphasis on still-life, figures and landscape.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: INTRODUCTION TO VIDEO
Course Description: Introduction to fundamentals of craft and study of experimental video. Emphasis on developing ideas and conveying meaning through video art, working outside commercial traditions.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: INTRO TO ANIMATION
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: An introduction to the history, tools and language of basic animation styles. This course will trace the history of experiments in animated imagery from 19th Century photography through 20th Century film into 21st Century digital works. The class will cover basic techniques in Photoshop, Adobe Premier, and illustration and animation software interfaces.

TITLE: INTRO TO PRINTMAKING
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Sophomores, & Juniors only.
Course Description: Exploration of printmaking's interdisciplinary nature, blending drawing and painting via traditional methods including notan, rubbings, monoprint, monotype, suminagashi, linocut, and woodcut. Production of relief prints, carved blocks, print editions and an accordion book.
Notes: Not open to seniors.

TITLE: ADV PHOTO:ANALOG TECH
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., and Sophomores.
Course Description: Advanced investigation and study of the creative tools of black-and-white photography through the use of analog film cameras. Emphasis on medium and large format cameras, studio techniques and darkroom printing. Continued exploration of personal vision with emphasis on social and cultural contexts for photography.
Notes: Normally offered every 3rd year.

TITLE: ADV PAINT: FIGURATION
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: This course develops basic paint handling, visual syntax, and conceptual abilities pertaining to the figure in space. Students will examine historical and contemporary methods.  Students will gain an appreciation of the physicality, emotional touchstones, and communicative power of paint. Students will explore varied genres within representation. including contemporary portraiture, history painting, the nude, and self portraiture.

TITLE: ADVANCED SCULPTURE
Course Description: This course explores form, surface and content at an advanced level, questioning how sculpture can most effectively engage the viewer’s mind and body. Students will develop their own studio practices while experimenting with a broad range of techniques, including carving in wood and wax; mold-making and casting in plaster, resin, and silicone; and digital rendering and 3D printing.

TITLE: SENIOR PROJECT EXHIBITION
COMMENTS: Open to Seniors Only.
Course Description: A course for senior concentrators in which students finalize their work from ART-501 for presentation in the Wellin Museum. Students will learn exhibition design, presentation issues for museum exhibition, installation techniques, working with galleries and museums, writing of artist statement and label text, documentation of 2D and 3D work, and basic website design.
Prerequisite Narrative: ART-501 with a minimum grade of A- and departmental approval

TITLE: INTRODUCTION TO ART HISTORY
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Years.
Course Description: This course is an introduction to the production, reception, and circulation of art in the modern world, from roughly 1450 to the present. We will examine art in its social, economic, and political context, while focusing on themes of artistic mobility and collaboration, as well as exchanges across cultures and media. Students will gain a basic understanding of visual vocabulary and literacy, and develop visual analysis skills by working with objects in campus and local collections.

TITLE: ART OF ADVERTISING
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores only.
Course Description: Advertising images are everywhere, beckoning us to look and believe their message. But how do such images actually work, and where do their visual strategies come from? This writing-intensive seminar equips students with the foundational skills of visual and contextual analysis necessary for the study of art and visual media. We will study how artists, designers, photographers, and advertising professionals created influential campaigns in print, on television, and online. Students will learn to analyze how images and text work together, how ads capture our attention, how they borrow from different visual traditions, and how they shape our desires, often through troubling visual conventions.

TITLE: INTERSECTIONS GLOBAL ART
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores Only.
Course Description: In this course we will look closely at 25 objects (roughly one per day) that embody significant intersections among different cultures and/or periods. We will be learning about how to look at works of art and how to effectively express our thoughts about them in spoken and written words. All class sessions will be held at the Wellin Museum of Art, Burke Special Collections, or the College Archives to guide our object-based study.

TITLE: ARTIFACT TESTAMENT & MONUMENT
Course Name: Artifact, Testament, and Monument: Asian Art Histories
Course Description: An introduction to the rich art histories of Asia from the prehistoric period to the present, with an emphasis on the arts of China, Japan, Korea, India, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and Indonesia. With the study of select objects, paintings, sculptures, monuments, and associated social, religious, and political milieus, students will be introduced to major styles and traditions in the history of art across Asia and will engage with critical themes in the interpretation of Asian art histories.

TITLE: BLACK CONCEPTUALISM
Course Description: From the 1960s to the present, Black artists have played a leading role in developing the experimental techniques of conceptual art. Across the Americas, Europe, and Africa, Black artists moved beyond traditional mediums like painting and sculpture to create artworks in the form of typewritten texts, logical systems, philosophical treatises, historical archives, video installations, and street performances. These methods were tied to a wide range of themes: the critique of racist institutions, research into suppressed histories, explorations of postcolonial and diasporic identity, and the embodied experiences of gender and sexuality. Readings will be drawn from art history, artists’ writings, and interdisciplinary scholarship in Black Studies.

TITLE: BUILDING JERUSALEM
Course Name: Building Jerusalem: The Making and Remaking of a Holy City
Course Description: Since its foundation, the city of Jerusalem has been claimed materially and spiritually by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. This course will, through its art and architecture, trace the complex history of Jerusalem from ca. 957 BCE to today’s divided city. The art and architecture of the city is contextualized in a way that speaks beyond the often-used and simplistic tripartite manner of constructing identity and history in the city.

TITLE: NORTHERN RENAISSANCE ART
Course Description: This course explores the distinctive ways in which art was crafted and consumed in northern Europe during the age of Renaissance and Reformation. We will examine paintings and prints, propaganda and princely splendor, and carved altarpieces and ceremonial armor against the backdrop of both city and court, while considering issues of religious function, social use, and the economic history of the arts. The course also fosters a critical awareness of the methods of art history by drawing attention to scholarship on Northern art that has, in many ways, laid the foundations for modernity.

TITLE: GLOBAL CONTEMPORARY ART
Course Description: Global Contemporary Art surveys the expanding definitions, contexts, and forms of art in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, paying particular attention to the significance of artistic agency, artists’ writings, globalization, the art market, and political engagement and social transformation.

TITLE: AVANT GARDE CINEMA
Course Name: Avant Garde: Cinema as Theory and Critique
Course Description: A history of alternatives to commercial movies, focusing on surrealist and dadaist film, visual music, psychodrama, direct cinema, the film society movement,  personal cinema, the New American Cinema, structuralism, Queer cinema, feminist cinema, minor cinema, recycled cinema and devotional cinema.  While conventional entertainment films use the novel, the short story and the stage drama as their primary instigations, experimental and avant-garde films are analogous to music, poetry, painting, sculpture and collage.
Notes: Not open to first-year students.

TITLE: EPIC TALES
Course Name: Epic Tales: Storytelling in South Asian Art
Course Description: South Asia’s extensive corpus of epics, fables, popular tales, and romances have found spirited visual expression in the region’s history of art and architecture. This seminar will analyze artistic choice and the role that it plays in how words are visually translated into images. We will examine a range of case studies from a period spanning over two thousand years to understand how artists shaped space, unfurled time, and materialized heroes and villains in painting and sculpture.

TITLE: ANTHROPOCENE AESTHETICS
Course Description: This seminar in contemporary art history and theory explores ecological art in the era of anthropogenic climate change. The course’s guiding question will be: what forms might an aesthetic experience of nature take when it no longer privileges the human observer, but rather cultivates an equality and reciprocity among all forms of life? Possible answers will be drawn from recent work in art history, Black studies, Indigenous studies, continental philosophy, and science and technology studies. The course’s topics will include: post-Enlightenment aesthetics of nature, biopower, vitalism, post- and anti-humanisms, plant philosophies, bacteria and fungi studies, and deep time. These theoretical frameworks will be complemented with case studies on a global array of contemporary artists.
Notes: Not open to first year students.

TITLE: POSTCOL THEORY & ISLAMIC ART
Course Description: How does the study of art and architectural history interface with colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial structures of power? This is a pressing question for those who study the visual cultures of the Middle East, a region in which these power structures have had considerable impact historically as well as in the contemporary moment. This class will consider from theoretical and practical vantage points how colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial systems and institutions have governed or influenced the methods of study, scope, and modes of display of historical art from the Middle East. Topics will include colonial-era collection and museum practices, Orientalism and its critics, post-colonial nationalist art historical discourses, cultural heritage in and during the ‘wars on terror’, and visual discourses of contemporary Islamophobia. Students may pursue research projects with objects or items from the Wellin Museum and/or the Michael Lang ’67 Special Collections and Archives.

TITLE: SACRED IN SOUTH ASIA
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Years, Sophomores, and Juniors.
Course Description: What constitutes the sacred in south Asia? Is it a person, place, river, hill, temple or nature/ecology? Where and how did the notion of sacrality emerge in South Asia? Is it linked exclusively to religious institutions or is it found in the daily lives of people? This course will examine these questions by exploring the multiple religious traditions of South Asia and examining their essential beliefs, doctrines, institutions, rituals and popular practices through a study of texts, material culture, films and ethnographic accounts.

TITLE: SAGES OF THE TAO IN CHINA
Course Name: Sages of the Tao in Chinese History
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, and 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Examination of the two most significant sages in Chinese history and the disciples and schools that traced their origins to them. Close readings of texts attributed to Laozi and Confucius, the conflicting interpretations of their teachings throughout Chinese history, and the proliferation of schools that claimed to transmit their Tao. An eminent historian once said, “Every era has its own Confucius; it’s just that there are many different Confucius[es] in any one era.” This adage, as we shall see, applies to Laozi as well.

TITLE: ARTIFACT TESTAMENT & MONUMENT
Course Name: Artifact, Testament, and Monument: Asian Art Histories
Course Description: An introduction to the rich art histories of Asia from the prehistoric period to the present, with an emphasis on the arts of China, Japan, Korea, India, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and Indonesia. With the study of select objects, paintings, sculptures, monuments, and associated social, religious, and political milieus, students will be introduced to major styles and traditions in the history of art across Asia and will engage with critical themes in the interpretation of Asian art histories.

TITLE: RESISTANCE HISTORY THRU FILM
Course Name: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

TITLE: MOTHER NATURE
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: How have people in India understood and interacted with mother nature? How do they conceptualize the environment and ecosystems? How do they deal with climate change and ecological disasters? What role does religion play in shaping human attitude to the mother nature? Focusing on Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, the course examines how Indian communities have engaged and negotiated their relationships with the natural world to consider themes including the conception of environment as sacred space, ethical living, non-violence, animal-protection, and food-culture.
Notes: No prior coursework on Religion or Asia is required.

TITLE: GUNPOWDER ISLAM
Course Name: Gunpowder Islam: Empires in Turkey, Iran, and India, c.1500-1800
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Fifty years ago, the scholar Marshall Hodgson coined the term "gunpowder empires" to describe the introduction of new military technology by early modern Islamic kingdoms across Eurasia, specifically in Turkey, Iran, and India. Using this cultural framework to study the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal Empires, this course will focus on issues of imperial power and expansion, social and religious authority, protest and dissent, language and literature, law and ethics, paintings and architecture, as well as gender and sexuality. We will explore the historiography of these Islamic polities along with reading primary sources including court chronicles, local histories, political treatises, religious texts, and poetry in Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit, Hindavi and other languages.

TITLE: GLOBAL ASIA
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: This methods course is designed to introduce students to the theoretical and conceptual frameworks to study Asia. This course will adopt an interdisciplinary and comparative lens to study multiple regions, cultures, and histories of East, South and West Asia. How are the particularities of Asian identity reflected in visual cultures? In what ways have scholars evaluated textual and material sources to study different Asian religions such as Buddhism, Islam, Hinduism and Confucianism? How has the colonial experience shaped periodization debates, modernity, and everyday life in countries like India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Myanmar? We will examine the diversity of Asian languages and literatures in translation, as well as global and transregional connections evident in travelogues, trade networks, and musical exchanges.

TITLE: EPIC TALES
Course Name: Epic Tales: Storytelling in South Asian Art
Course Description: South Asia’s extensive corpus of epics, fables, popular tales, and romances have found spirited visual expression in the region’s history of art and architecture. This seminar will analyze artistic choice and the role that it plays in how words are visually translated into images. We will examine a range of case studies from a period spanning over two thousand years to understand how artists shaped space, unfurled time, and materialized heroes and villains in painting and sculpture. This class has no prerequisites.

TITLE: MADNESS, LOVESICKNESS, & JINN
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. First Years require instructor permission.
Course Description: “Madness” evokes images of rambling, potentially violent, individuals on the margins of society. How did historical attitudes to insanity evolve in early modern and modern Eurasia? Were madpeople always ostracized or were they simply objects of sympathy and pity? What did hospitals and other networks of care and healing look like for mentally ill patients? In poetry, the pain of separation of the lover from their beloved produced lovesickness. Finally, demonic possession of the brain by jinns (Islamic spirits) was thought to cause madness. How can we understand the literary, religious and supernatural world of these actors without dismissing it? This course will take a holistic view of insanity while engaging with the rise of asylums or other lunatic institutions.

TITLE: BIOLOGICAL CHEMISTRY
Course Description: A survey of the chemical and physical nature of biological macromolecules, including nucleic acids, proteins, lipids and carbohydrates; biochemistry of enzyme catalysis; bioenergetics and regulatory mechanisms. Principles and techniques of experimental biochemistry, focusing on isolation methods and techniques for analyzing structure and function. This course satisfies the second semester of a one-year General Chemistry requirement for post-graduate Health Professions programs, however, this course might not also satisfy a Health Profession program’s requirement for a course in Biochemistry.
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

TITLE: EXB: FRANKENSTEIN FISH
Course Description: A thematic course exploring five fundamental features of all biological systems, including structure and function, information flow, energy and matter, interactions, and evolution. As humans continue to exploit the ocean’s resources by overfishing, aquaculture and mariculture have become more and more important to meet human demands for fish proteins. This course will examine overfishing, genetically modified/engineered foods, and animal cloning and engineering to introduce fundamental concepts of ecology, ecosystems and conservation biology, genetics and molecular biology, and ethical issues.
Notes: Students must concurrently enroll in a Bio100L lab section.  Not open to students who have taken any other Explorations in Biology course.

TITLE: EXB: EVOLUTION OF SEX
Course Name: Explorations in Biology: The Evolution of Sex
COMMENTS: Open to Seniors, Juniors, Sophomores, & 1st Years. Not open to those who took BIO 100*. Must also sign up for a BIO-100L section.
Course Description: A thematic course exploring five fundamental features of all biological systems, including structure and function, information flow, energy and matter, interactions, and evolution. How did sexual reproduction evolve? Why don’t all animals make clonal copies of themselves? How does sex shape selection and the evolution of plants and animals? How does sex influence human life and society? These are some of the questions this course will explore as we dive into understanding the origins of sexual reproduction across the animal tree of life.
Notes: Students must concurrently enroll in a BIO 100L lab section. Not open to students who have taken any other Explorations in Biology course.

TITLE: MICROSCOPY FUNDAMENTALS
Course Description: This course is a broad introduction to many common types of microscopy (bright field, confocal microscopy, electron microscopy). In addition to learning the theoretical foundations, students will also get hands-on practice with microscopes throughout the semester. The course will also cover the basics of digital image acquisition, processing, and analysis. Three hours a week, split between class and lab.

TITLE: BIOMATERIALS
Course Description: Plants and animals create materials to accomplish their complex goals for survival and reproduction. These biological materials, from wood to silk to shells to fur, have diverse and unique physical properties. This course will explore the physical/engineering properties of biological materials. We will learn the basics of structural mechanics while asking how and why organisms create these materials.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any BIO-100 or consent of the instructor

TITLE: ECOLOGY & EVOLUTIONARY BIO
Course Description: An intermediate course that provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental principles of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, emphasizing their deep interconnectedness. Students will explore the mechanisms of ecology and evolution, spanning from molecular-level changes to population, community, and ecosystem phenomena. Students will develop analytical and quantitative tools to solve real-world ecological and evolutionary problems. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Corequisite Narrative: Must be taken with BIO 210 lab section
Usual instructor: Andrea Townsend, Ariel Kahrl, Pete Guiden
Notes: Not open to those who took BIO 237 or BIO 250. Must also register for BIO 210 lab section.

TITLE: GENES, MOLECULES, & CELLS
COMMENTS: Open to Sophomores and 1st Yrs only. Not open to those who took BIO 248. Must also register for BIO 211 lab section.
Course Description: An intermediate course that examines genetics and biochemistry within the context of the cell. This course will focus on the macromolecules of life, genetic material and classical genetics, fundamental biochemical pathways, and cellular structure and function. A particular focus will be placed on proteins and nucleic acids and how cells use these molecules to direct the mechanisms of inheritance, energy production, and cellular reproduction. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisites: BIO-100A, , BIO-100B, , BIO-100D, , BIO-100E, , BIO-100F, , BIO-100G, , BIO-100H, , BIO 100I, , BIO-100J, , BIO-100K,

TITLE: MICROBIOLOGY
Course Description: Introduction to microorganisms, including bacteria, archaea, single-cell eukaryotes (yeast, algae, protozoa) and viruses, with an emphasis on prokaryotic metabolism and ecology. Basic laboratory techniques, including isolation, cultivation and characterization of microbes. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: BIO-100, 101, 102, or 115 and CHEM-120 or CHEM-125; or consent of instructor

TITLE: HUMAN ANATOMY
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Exploration of the structure and function of human tissues, organs and systems with an introduction to basic pathology and diagnostic tools. This course emphasizes physiological function and the role of anatomical form in these processes. Examines skeletal, muscular, endocrine, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and reproductive systems of humans. Thoughtful dissections of animal model systems and analysis of histology will be the focus of the laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any BIO-100 or consent of instructor
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

TITLE: INVERTEBRATE BIOLOGY
Course Description: Survey of animal diversity, including marine and freshwater fauna, parasites, insects and the origin of vertebrates. Emphasis on morphology, physiology, ecology and evolution. Three hours of class, three hours of laboratory.

Course Description: This course will cover the fundamental principles of evolution starting with the processes that generate variation within and between populations and building up to the patterns that result in speciation and macroevolution. Students will spend the semester learning this material while engaging in research projects that involve data analysis, visual and oral communication, and extensive scientific writing.

TITLE: IMMUNOLOGY
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores.
Course Description: This course introduces the cellular and molecular mechanisms of vertebrate immunity in health and disease. Topics include the evolution and organization of the immune system, innate and adaptive immune responses, immune cell development and communication, and the dysregulation and therapeutic manipulation of immune responses. Lectures, case studies, and primary literature will be used to explore fundamental immunological concepts and their applications to human health. Laboratory experiments will examine immune cell function and introduce current immunological techniques through guided exercises and independent projects.
Notes: This course will have an accompanying three hours of laboratory work per week.

TITLE: SYSTEMS NEUROSCIENCE
Course Description: The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.

TITLE: SEM IN DISEASE & BEHAVIOR
Course Description: The relationship between animal behavior and disease is bidirectional: behavior can affect the likelihood of acquiring a disease, and disease can subsequently alter behavior. In this class, we examine the fundamentals of animal behavior (e.g., sexual selection, kin selection, social evolution, communication and signals, reproductive strategies) and apply them to current research on the ecology and evolution of disease. Discussion of foundational readings and the primary literature.
Notes: Students must have Junior or Senior standing.

TITLE: SEM IN CANCER BIOLOGY
Course Description: Why have we not cured cancer yet? There are many good ways to answer the question. By the end of this course, you will be able to articulate a dozen valid explanations and reframe these challenges as future research, healthcare, and policy goals. Through analysis and discussion of recent primary literature, we will explore the complex genetics and epigenetics of the group of diseases we call malignant neoplasms. Topics include mutations that drive tumor progression, phenotypes of malignant cells, interactions of cancer cells with their environment, techniques for studying cancer biology, and therapies used in modern oncology.

TITLE: SEM BIOINFORMATICS

Course Description: An integrated lecture-laboratory course in which students learn to design, build, and use instrumentation to study the physicochemical properties of atoms and molecules. Topics include the theory and practice of optical spectroscopy, thermochemical measurements of gases and condensed phases, and the measurement of reaction kinetics. Evaluations stress mastery of laboratory technique and communication of results with an emphasis on oral communication. Speaking-Intensive. One hour of lecture, three hours of laboratory.

COMMENTS: Restricted to CHEM majors. 0.5 credit course; runs 3/29/27-5/17/27.

TITLE: ENVIRON CHEM AND LIT
Course Name: The Road to Silent Spring and Beyond: The Intersections of Environmental Chemistry and Literature
Course Description: An exploration of how environmental chemistry shapes environmental literature. Course material will include primary chemical sources as well as essays, novels, short stories, film, and other environmental literature. This course will look at both natural environmental chemistry as well as the chemistry of anthropogenic changes and compounds, such as pesticides. Students will interrogate and discuss these connections then use them to discover their own intersections with chemistry and literature.
Prerequisite Narrative: One 200-level Environmental Studies or Chemistry course

TITLE: SCI, TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
COMMENTS: Restricted to CHEM and PHYS majors. 0.5 credit class; Runs from 1/20/27 to 3/12/27.
Course Description: An examination of the assumptions, paradigms, and hierarchies embedded in science and technology. This course will examine evidence pointing to the structure of hierarchies built into and from science and how those structures may result in inequalities for various groups participating in and affected by science and technology. Topics will vary but might include: the objectivity/subjectivity of science; how biases and social structures intersect with equity, diversity, and inclusion in science; and gender and race disparities in STEM fields.
Prerequisite Narrative: Restricted to Chemistry or Physics concentrators or permission of the instructor.

TITLE: ADVANCED ORGANIC SPECTROSCOPY
COMMENTS: 0.5 credit class; Runs from 1/20/27 to 3/12/27.
Course Description: A study of advanced topics in NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry with a focus on practical interpretation of spectra. Topics include NMR theory, chemical shift, spin-spin coupling, dynamic NMR, 2D NMR techniques (COSY, NOESY, HSQC/HMQC, HMBC), methods of ionization in mass spectrometry, and interpretation of mass spectral fragmentation patterns.
Notes: One-half credit.

TITLE: SECOND TERM CHINESE
Course Description: This course is the second semester in introductory level of Chinese. The course will cover the remaining five units (Unit 6-10) of the learning materials, Basic Mandarin Chinese (Speaking & Listening; Reading & Writing). The course will help students further develop skills in Mandarin Chinese to conduct basic communication across ethnic, cultural and ideological boundaries and to develop an understanding of Chinese interpersonal behavioral culture. At the end of the course, students will be expected to perform in speaking, listening, reading and writing Chinese at a level of proficiency appropriate for continuing on to the intermediate level of Chinese courses. They should also demonstrate a level of cultural understanding suitable for correct performance of assigned tasks in Chinese.

They should also demonstrate a level of cultural understanding suitable for correct performance of assigned tasks in Chinese.

TITLE: FOURTH TERM CHINESE
Course Description: Continuation of third-term Chinese. Development of spoken and written skills, as well as familiarity with current Chinese culture. Class discussions in Chinese. Four hours of class, with additional lab work and individual sessions for each student.

TITLE: ADVANCED CHINESE II
Course Description: Continuation of Advanced Chinese I, with emphasis on making the transition from textbook to an advanced level of competence for reading periodicals and journals in China. Discussion, written and oral work. Taught in Chinese.

TITLE: EAST ASIAN WOMEN IN FILM
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Years.
Course Description: This course examines portrayals of East Asian women in mainland Chinese, Hong Kong, Taiwanese, Japanese, Korean, and Hollywood films, with an emphasis on the post-#MeToo era. Through close analysis of narrative films and documentaries, students learn to investigate how gendered experiences of oppression, resilience, and resistance are represented, challenged, and reimagined in diverse cultural contexts. Combining film studies and gender studies, the course highlights both shared and divergent regional patterns and encourages students to consider how cinema shapes public debates on social change, agency, and justice. All films include English subtitles. Course requirements include film viewings, presentations, active discussion, a creative project, and a final paper.

TITLE: TAIWAN THROUGH FILM
Course Description: This course is an advanced-level Chinese language and Chinese-speaking culture course. It explores the complex cinematic depictions of Taiwan’s history, politics, and culture across the greater Chinese-speaking world. At the same time, it provides advanced-level Chinese language training. Through this dual focus, students will gain a nuanced perspective on Taiwan’s role in shaping cinematic narratives while gaining the language proficiency needed to participate fluently in discussions on both familiar and abstract topics, present structured arguments, and articulate in-depth analyses and sophisticated ideas in Chinese.

TITLE: ANCIENT GREEK HIST & CULTURE
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: An introduction to the legacy of ancient Greece through the study of history, literature, philosophy, and art. This course will also consider the influence of neighboring cultures on Ancient Greece, including the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and the Persians, to name a few.

TITLE: SOCIAL LIVES ANCIENT DEAD
Course Name: The Social Lives of the Ancient Dead
Course Description: What happened to people after they died in the ancient world? Often, their story was only beginning. This course looks at the ways the dead remained part of everyday life. We will read curse tablets that call on restless spirits, laws about stolen bodies, stories about cities fighting over heroic bones, and Christian accounts of remains that heal or protect the living. We will also study tombs and inscriptions to see how people used the dead to make claims about family, memory, status, and belonging. The course ends close to home. For the final project, students will turn to Hamilton’s own cemetery and investigate how one grave, monument, or burial story creates a social life for the dead on our campus. The larger question throughout the course is simple: what can the dead still do for the living?
Notes: (Application, Interpretation)

TITLE: RACE, ETHNICITY: GREECE, ROME
Course Name: Race and Ethnicity in Ancient Greece and Rome
COMMENTS: CLASC 227W is open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only. The 300-level is open to non-Justice Lab students with instructor's permission.
Course Description: In this course, we will examine social constructions of race and ethnicity in Ancient Greece and Rome. What evidence survives, both textual and material, and what challenges do we face in interpreting it? How do conceptions of race differ by place and time through the Greco-Roman world? What is the difference between race and ethnicity? How have ancient ideas of race and racial hierarchies influenced later ones, and how have modern ideas influenced our interpretations of the past?
Notes: This 200-level section is specifically designed to be part of a Justice Lab. Students who are interested in this course, but NOT planning to enroll in the Justice Lab, should consider the 300-level companion course, CLASC-327, offered by our department.

TITLE: RACE, ETHNICITY: GREECE, ROME
Course Name: Race and Ethnicity in Ancient Greece and Rome
COMMENTS: First Years require instructor permission.
Course Description: In this course, we will examine social constructions of race and ethnicity in Ancient Greece and Rome. What evidence survives, both textual and material, and what challenges do we face in interpreting it? How do conceptions of race differ by place and time through the Greco-Roman world? What is the difference between race and ethnicity? How have ancient ideas of race and racial hierarchy influenced later ones, and how have modern ideas influenced our interpretations of the past? This course requires no knowledge of Ancient Greek or Latin, but students with such knowledge can aid in our discussions of problems introduced by translations.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in GREEK, LATIN, CLASC, WMGST, AFRST or SOC-231
Notes: Students should expect to participate in daily discussion. The course was designed by multiple professors in the department and will be either team-taught, or taught by each professor in rotation.

TITLE: SENIOR PROGRAM
COMMENTS: Restricted to Senior Clasc Majors.
Course Description: Topics to be arranged.
Notes: Open only to senior concentrators.

TITLE: ART OF ADVERTISING
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores only.
Course Description: Advertising images are everywhere, beckoning us to look and believe their message. But how do such images actually work, and where do their visual strategies come from? This writing-intensive seminar equips students with the foundational skills of visual and contextual analysis necessary for the study of art and visual media. We will study how artists, designers, photographers, and advertising professionals created influential campaigns in print, on television, and online. Students will learn to analyze how images and text work together, how ads capture our attention, how they borrow from different visual traditions, and how they shape our desires, often through troubling visual conventions.

TITLE: WORLD FILMS, WORLD FAITHS
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: Introduces the practices and beliefs of several major world religions (including Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism) through the medium of film. Exploring Japanese anime, Indonesia documentaries, video films from Ghana, Bollywood mythologicals, Jesus-films from Latin America, Korean-Buddhist films, contemporary fictional glimpses into Jewish life, and more, shows how religious people live and struggle and find joy, by using the audio-visual medium of film.
Notes: Evening film screenings.

TITLE: BOLLYWOOD FILM
Course Description: The course charts a history of Bollywood, India’s mainstream Hindi-language film industry. Although dismissed for its use of melodrama and song-dance sequences, Bollywood has long engaged with other global cinemas and critiqued social, cultural, and political trends. Readings and films span romances about gender and nation like Mother India (1957) and Chaudhvin Ka Chand (1960); the 1970s "angry young man" oeuvre and its later avatars, crime and terrorist films; diasporic family dramas like Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003); and crossover hits like The Lunch Box (2013) that address the globalized present.
Notes: This course may be offered as writing-intensive or not writing-intensive, per the deparment. Refer to the schedule for details.

TITLE: RESISTANCE HISTORY THRU FILM
Course Name: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

TITLE: FILMS OF THE COEN BROTHERS
Course Name: The Films of the Coen Brothers: Genre and Pastiche at the end of the American Mythos
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
Course Description: This course will analyze the way the Coen Brothers’ films play with previously hegemonic myths about the American experience. How do their films negotiate expectations of genre? What happens to meaning when pastiche or appropriation become vital to the narrative and imaginary world of the films? We will watch up to a dozen films, including Fargo, No Country for Old Men, Miller’s Crossing, O Brother Where art Thou and The Big Lebowski, not quite in chronological order,. Readings from scholarly and theoretical material, as well as excerpts from many of their sources, from Homer to Hammett. We'll also consider some of the 20th century painting, architecture and style that informs their films. Mandatory out of class viewings.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Literature or Cinema and Media Studies, or permission of instructor
Notes: Theory, Intermedia

TITLE: EAST ASIAN WOMEN IN FILM
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Years.
