TITLE: ELEMENTARY ANCIENT GREEK
Course Description: An introduction to the language and culture of Greece and the ancient Mediterranean. Thorough grounding in the grammar, syntax and vocabulary of ancient Greek. Reading and discussion of elementary passages from classical or New Testament Greek that cast light on ancient Mediterranean society and culture. For those with no previous knowledge of Greek.
Notes: Three class meetings a week, in addition to a drill session.

TITLE: TOPIC: THE HOLY DEAD
Course Name: Topics in Ancient Greek Society and Culture
Course Description: Reading and discussion of original Greek texts that cast light on the history, society and culture of Greece and the ancient Mediterranean. Authors and topics vary.
Notes: May be retaken for credit.

TITLE: US BORDERLANDS
Course Name: Borders and Borderlands in US History
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: This course asks how territorial boundaries have evolved into a dispersed, interior regime of surveillance and control over the course of American history. Beginning with colonial-era treaties and other practices of boundary-making in early US history, we will turn to examine U.S.–Mexico borderlands as a region shaped not only by movement, exchange, and cultural intermingling, but also by the evolving power of the state and the contested processes of border‑making. Special emphasis will be given to the intertwined histories of Indigenous, Mexican, Black, Chinese, and Euro‑American communities and to examining how borders are produced, negotiated, and lived, while developing critical reading and writing skills in history.

TITLE: EARLY MOD WESTERN EUROPE
Course Description: Survey of transformation of Western Europe from the Renaissance through the French Revolution. Focuses on social, political, economic and intellectual developments; examination of primary sources and secondary studies. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.

TITLE: INTRO U.S. HIST 1861-2001
Course Name: An Introduction to the History of the United States, 1861-2001.
Course Description: Introduction to U.S. history and an overview of the Civil War and Reconstruction, the emergence of the U.S. as a global power, progressivism and the New Deal, the Cold War, the liberal and radical insurgencies of the 1960s, and the conservative revival of the 1970s to the present.

TITLE: BLACK POWER MOVEMENT
Course Description: The course will focus on the political history of the Black Power Movement. By 1966, Black Power advocates charged by Stokely Carmichael and the Black Panthers, began a series of meetings with the help of Black politicians like Adam Clayton Powell. By 1967 and 1968, these same activists began planning, holding, and developing rallies for a new U.S. constitutional convention. This class is a political and intellectual history on the legacy of the Black Power Movement, its organizations, leaders, and ideologies. The course seeks to uncover the intellectual history of Black Power as a movement for democratic practice and multiracial democracy in the United States.

TITLE: ANCIENT GREEK HIST & CULTURE
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: An introduction to the legacy of ancient Greece through the study of history, literature, philosophy, and art. This course will also consider the influence of neighboring cultures on Ancient Greece, including the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and the Persians, to name a few.

TITLE: MEDIEVAL CHRISTIANITIES
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Sophomores, & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: A survey of the development of the Christian religion in premodern Eurasia and the Mediterranean, from its elevation to a state cult in the later Roman Empire to about 1450. Special consideration will be given to the growth of the church and processes of conversion, the problem of authority versus heresy and heterodoxy, and the relationship of the Christian churches to Islam and other non-Christian peoples. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.

TITLE: GLOBAL HISTORY OF OIL
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: How was our current dependence on petroleum created, and how can historical thinking help us imagine a better future? This course combines approaches from environmental and social history to examine the oil industry from the 19th century to today.  Students explore social and environmental justice movements, the lives of oil industry workers, and our changing global economy, emphasizing peoples and places that are often marginalized.  Contribute to contemporary debates on fossil fuels by analyzing museum exhibits in a final writing project.

TITLE: SAGES OF THE TAO IN CHINA
Course Name: Sages of the Tao in Chinese History
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, and 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Examination of the two most significant sages in Chinese history and the disciples and schools that traced their origins to them. Close readings of texts attributed to Laozi and Confucius, the conflicting interpretations of their teachings throughout Chinese history, and the proliferation of schools that claimed to transmit their Tao. An eminent historian once said, “Every era has its own Confucius; it’s just that there are many different Confucius[es] in any one era.” This adage, as we shall see, applies to Laozi as well.

TITLE: THE AMERICAN CIVIL WAR
Course Description: Examines the causes, conduct and legacy of the American Civil War, with particular attention to the debate over slavery, the divergent social, economic and cultural development of the southern and northern states, the religious dimension of the war, battle front strategy and home front mobilization, the politics of emancipation, reconstruction, redemption and reconciliation, and the Civil War in popular memory down to the present.

TITLE: MODERN RUSSIAN HISTORY
Course Description: An overview of Russian history from the emancipation of the serfs to the collapse of the Soviet Union. Themes of the course include how Russia and the USSR dealt with their sense of "backwardness" compared to Europe, the multi-national and multi-religious nature of this vast Eurasian state, and the meanings of "modernity."

TITLE: GENDER&VIOLENCE MIDDLE AGES
Course Name: Gender and Violence in the Middle Ages
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: This course serves as an introduction to the field of Medieval and Renaissance Studies. Drawing on multiple disciplinary perspectives, including those of literature, law, history, and art, we will examine the intersection of ideas about the body, gender, and violence in the European Middle Ages. Readings may include the Bible and early patristic writings; the lives of saints; poems and advice manuals on courtly love; depictions of women in the Crusades; Icelandic sagas; and perspectives on the trial of Joan of Arc.
Prerequisite Narrative: One 100-level course in literature or history, or AP 4 or 5 in English or history.
Notes: (History).

TITLE: ENGLAND,IRELAND 1485-1701
Course Description: This course examines the shifting boundaries of sovereignty and religion in Britain and Ireland in the period from the founding of the Tudor monarchy to the Glorious Revolution.  It simultaneously shows how England developed its power overseas through trade, colonization, and privateering.  This course illuminates the disparate, multicultural societies over which the English monarchy extended its rule, demonstrating how tumultuous struggles to consolidate and sustain political authority in the ‘Atlantic archipelago’ corresponded with the global expansion of British commerce.

TITLE: RESISTANCE HISTORY THRU FILM
Course Name: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

TITLE: RECENT AMERICAN HIST
Course Name: Recent American History: The United States, 1941 to the Present
Course Description: A survey of American political, economic, cultural and social life from the start of the Second World War to the present. Topics include the Second World War, the Cold War, McCarthyism, the Civil Rights Movement, the sixties and their aftermath, and the Reagan Revolution and its aftermath.

TITLE: EARLY REPUBLIC: 1800-1840
Course Name: The Early Republic, 1800 to 1840: From Jefferson to Jackson
Course Description: An intensive examination of the political, social, cultural, and economic history of the United States from the election of Jefferson to 1840. Focus on Jefferson's presidency, Lewis and Clark expedition, War of 1812, Second Great Awakening, slavery and its expansion, growth of antislavery and abolition, Indian removal, foreign relations, and the Market Revolution.

TITLE: AFRICAN-AMERICAN POL HISTORY
Course Description: This class is a survey of the role of African Americans in American electoral politics from Reconstruction to the 21st century and seeks to help students understand how Black people have navigated both mainstream and radical political ideologies to claim their citizenship in a multiracial democracy.

TITLE: COMMON GROUND
Course Name: Common Ground: A Laboratory for Civil Discourse
Course Description: Common Ground will be a speaking intensive, history and government class where students learn about the history of free speech in America and on campus through practicums. While engaging with the history, students will learn to disagree, agreeably through different exercises focusing on the U.S. Constitution in a "Reacting to the Past" role-playing game, a LLM for the Founding Fathers, and free speech on campus issues, especially the 2005 Ward Churchill incident that roiled the Hamilton campus.

TITLE: MODERN CHINA
Course Description: Examination of the social and cultural forces contributing to the decline of imperial institutions beginning in the 19th century, as found in the Taiping Rebellion, cultural interaction with Western missionaries, traders, and military and nationalist revolutions in the 20th century. Readings and class discussions consider the coherence of nationhood in Chinese identity and reexamine the "Western impact" as a force in the formation of modernism in China.

TITLE: THE CORPORATION
Course Description: The Corporation examines how corporations have evolved as economic, political, and cultural institutions, shaping and reflecting the societies in which they operate. Drawing on historical analysis and ethnographic perspectives, the course traces their development from early chartered companies to the 2008 financial crisis, exploring key transformations in corporate structure, legal personhood, and financialization. We will consider how corporations have been shaped by historical forces such as colonialism, industrialization, and neoliberalism, while also analyzing their cultural logics, organizational practices, and symbolic power. Readings will examine how corporations have reshaped labor, culture, and economic inequality, as well as the ways they have been challenged and reformed. By examining corporate influence across time and space, students will gain a deeper understanding of its role in the modern world.

TITLE: GUNPOWDER ISLAM
Course Name: Gunpowder Islam: Empires in Turkey, Iran, and India, c.1500-1800
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Fifty years ago, the scholar Marshall Hodgson coined the term "gunpowder empires" to describe the introduction of new military technology by early modern Islamic kingdoms across Eurasia, specifically in Turkey, Iran, and India. Using this cultural framework to study the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal Empires, this course will focus on issues of imperial power and expansion, social and religious authority, protest and dissent, language and literature, law and ethics, paintings and architecture, as well as gender and sexuality. We will explore the historiography of these Islamic polities along with reading primary sources including court chronicles, local histories, political treatises, religious texts, and poetry in Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit, Hindavi and other languages.

TITLE: WONDER & CERTAINTY
Course Name: Wonder and Certainty in Science and Religion
Course Description: Are we the only rational beings in the universe? Is such a thing as a soul? Can we predict the future? The truism goes that history is told by the victors, and the same is true for the history of ideas -- so, join us for a journey into the history of ideas that haven't made it into modern textbooks. Featuring materials from Hamilton College’s Special Collections, this course focuses on a series of case studies from early modern Europe and the Atlantic world that represent pivot points to teleologies in the history of science and thought. The result is a history of wonderment followed by doubt, illuminating divergent and sometimes abandoned paths once frequented by the wisest among humankind.

TITLE: PIETY, POWER, AND POLITICS
Course Name: Piety, Power, and Politics: Christianity in America, 1600-1890
Course Description: Examination of Christianity in America from the era of European settlement to the end of the 19th century.  Topics include encounters with Native American religions, revivalism, sectarianism, slavery and antislavery, religion and politics, theological developments, popular beliefs and practices, and the rise of unbelief.

TITLE: TOPIC: ARCHIVE & HISTORIANS
Course Description: This course examines how histories of borderlands and margins, emanating from empires and nationstates, turn them into simultaneous objects of desire and control. Through the example of Kashmir — long conceptualized as a famed paradisiacal land, which in the postcolonial era turned into a politically disputed and a heavily militarized zone — we will critically parse orientalist, nationalist, academic, and popular histories about such regions in South Asia and beyond. Building upon comparisons with similarly contested sites such as Palestine, the course will center a people’s understanding of history through counter historical narratives, literary works, protest music, and poetry.
Notes: Students in this course can opt-in for co-requisite archival research for an extra 0.5 course credit (HIST-183 History Workshop: Archival Practice and Theory).

TITLE: ARABS & JEWS MIDDLE EAST
Course Name: Arabs and Jews in the Middle East
Course Description: Deep study of the Arab-Israeli conflict from the 1880s to the present. We will study the relations between Arab and Jewish communities, the roots of Zionism, Western imperialism, and Israeli and Palestinian social and political evolution.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any 200-level history course, GOVT-207, or permission of the instructor

TITLE: HIMALAYAN MOUNTAINEERING
Course Name: The History and Literature of Himalayan Mountaineering, from the 19th Century to the Present.
COMMENTS: Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
Course Description: Examines Himalayan mountaineering over the past 150 years, and its roots in imperial expansion, national rivalries, and cultural and social evolution. Topics include mountaineering in the age of empire, George Leigh-Mallory’s death on Everest, American mountaineering in the Himalaya, conquest of the 8,000 meter peaks, the role of Sherpas in mountaineering, and the rise of commercial mountaineering.  (Writing-intensive.) There will be an optional 2-week field trip to the Annapurna region of Nepal over spring break, conditions permitting.  Generous travel aid is available to make the trip affordable to all students in the course.

TITLE: HISTORIES OF PHOTOGRAPHY
Course Name: Topics in British and Irish History: Photography in Britain and the Empire
Course Description: This research seminar examines photographs as historical texts.  It addresses changing photographic technologies and the many uses of photography in Britain and the Empire from visual art and scientific research to philanthropy and the categorization of criminals. Particular emphasis will be placed on photography’s role in representing and influencing ideas about class, race, and gender.
Prerequisite Narrative: one 200-level history course, or consent of the instructor.

TITLE: DUBOIS AND BLACK INTELLECTUAL
Course Name: W.E.B. Du Bois and the Black Intellectual Tradition
Course Description: This course will center the work of sociologist W.E.B. Du Bois and the intellectual history of Black radical thinkers in the 19th and twentieth century of the United States of America. The class will engage students with Du Bois' seminal work, Black Reconstruction in America: 1860 - 1880. The course is designed to examine the history of Black intellectual thought and activism in the United States from 1865 through 2000. With Du Bois guiding the course, students will be introduced to a wide range of Black radical thinkers through American history. Students will analyze how Du Bois' political transformation throughout several decades reflects similar crises experienced by the nation’s Black intellectuals as they tried to recover and rebuild Reconstruction.

TITLE: SENIOR SEMINAR
COMMENTS: Open to Senior HIST Concentrators only.
Course Description: This is part two of the senior project sequence. Students will research and write an article-length manuscript based on their proposal from HIST 450. Following the completion of thesis drafts, every student will participate in an oral defense of their thesis.

TITLE: SECOND TERM SPANISH
Course Description: Second Term Spanish continues to build language skills and intercultural competence for students who have taken one semester of college-level Spanish (HSPST 110) or its equivalent previously. The course reviews basic grammatical concepts and introduces the more advanced ones, interweaving language study with cultural studies of the Spanish-speaking world. The course develops proficiency in speaking, listening, reading, and writing in Spanish with the goal of reaching intermediate level by the end of the semester.
Notes: Course meets MWF for 50 minutes plus a weekly TA session (50 minutes).

TITLE: SECOND TERM SPANISH
Course Description: Second Term Spanish continues to build language skills and intercultural competence for students who have taken one semester of college-level Spanish (HSPST 110) or its equivalent previously. The course reviews basic grammatical concepts and introduces the more advanced ones, interweaving language study with cultural studies of the Spanish-speaking world. The course develops proficiency in speaking, listening, reading, and writing in Spanish with the goal of reaching intermediate level by the end of the semester.
Notes: Course meets MWF for 50 minutes plus a weekly TA session (50 minutes).

TITLE: FOURTH TERM SPANISH
Course Description: An advanced language course designed to strengthen and develop oral communication and writing skills. Conversation and debate play a central role and provide a framework for engaging with cultural topics and contemporary issues in the Spanish-speaking world. The course offers a rigorous review of Spanish grammar and seeks to refine students’ written expression through an array of formats including argumentative compositions, descriptive essays, creative narration, newspaper articles, and reviews.
Prerequisite Narrative: Grade of C or better in HSPST-130 or HSPST-135, placement exam, or consent of instructor. Not open to students who have taken HSPST-140.
Notes: Three hours of class weekly, with an additional weekly TA session. Taught in Spanish.

TITLE: EXPLORING HISPANIC TEXTS
COMMENTS: Not Open to Those Who Took Hspst-201W Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Introductory study of literature and culture from the Hispanic world (Spain, Latin America, and Hispanic United States), with an emphasis on refining oral and written skills in Spanish. Focus on written and oral argumentation, and textual analysis of various literary genres, including narrative, poetry, essay and drama. Additional cultural material studied includes film, art, music, and contemporary social issues. Advanced grammar in context and vocabulary building.
Prerequisite Narrative: Grade of C+ or better in HSPST 150 or 151, placement or consent of instructor
Notes: Taught in Spanish.

TITLE: EXPLORING HISPANIC TEXTS
COMMENTS: Not Open to Those Who Took Hspst-201W Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Introductory study of literature and culture from the Hispanic world (Spain, Latin America, and Hispanic United States), with an emphasis on refining oral and written skills in Spanish. Focus on written and oral argumentation, and textual analysis of various literary genres, including narrative, poetry, essay and drama. Additional cultural material studied includes film, art, music, and contemporary social issues. Advanced grammar in context and vocabulary building.
Prerequisite Narrative: Grade of C+ or better in HSPST 150 or 151, placement or consent of instructor
Notes: Taught in Spanish.

TITLE: SPANISH LITERATURE
Course Description: Intensive study and analysis of cultural concepts and selected literary works of Spain. Introduction to basic critical skills for literary and cultural analysis as applied to texts studied. Emphasis on oral performance, student participation and on original application of critical methodology in writing projects. The course includes a required one-day (Saturday) trip to New York City to see a Spanish performance.
Notes: Taught in Spanish. Not open to senior concentrators.

TITLE: INTRO U.S. LATINX/LIT
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: Examines cultural production of representative U.S. Latinx writers primarily from the civil rights movement to present. The course explores Latinx writers’ engagement with language, political status, race, gender, nationality, and generational markers to reveal both the fluidity and instability of the Latinx imaginary. Readings include autobiographical and biographical works, bildungsroman, memoir, historical novel and vignettes in an exploration of the self and one’s relation to collective identity.
Notes: Taught in English. Not open to seniors.

TITLE: INTRO HISPANIC CINEMA
COMMENTS: Taught in Spanish.
Course Description: An introduction to film in the Hispanic world, exploring the development of different national traditions within Latin American and Spanish Cinema. At the same time, covers some of the basic tools for interpreting and writing about film. Editing, sound, cinematography and mise-en-scène are some of the key terms and concepts studied in order to understand how viewers and filmmakers create meaning in films. Particular attention  to the interrelation of cinema and culture, and the intersection of aesthetics and politics.
Notes: Taught in Spanish.

TITLE: TRANSATLANTIC SURREALISM
Course Description: Dreams, the unconscious, and a 106,460,000 km² body of water we know as the Atlantic Ocean. Originally founded as a poetic movement in France, Surrealism quickly traveled across borders and creative disciplines, transforming beyond its revolutionary roots of the 1920s and 1930s. Using poetic thought, this course traces Hispanic Surrealism’s flux between Europe and Latin America, starting with its premodern predecessors before turning to its avant-garde rupture, and ending with its contemporary creators. Materials studied include poetry, cinema, and visual art.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in HSPST or SPAIN at the 200 level or above, or consent of instructor.
Notes: Taught in Spanish.

TITLE: CINEMA OF ICIAR BOLLAIN
Course Description: Study of the work of Spanish filmmaker and actress Icíar Bollaín (Madrid, 1967), exploring a wide spectrum of cultural, historical, and sociopolitical themes related to contemporary Spain (1980s-today). From her directorial debut, Hola, ¿estás sola? (1995), these themes will be examined through films such as Te doy mis ojos (2002), También la lluvia (2010), El olivo (2016), and Maixabel (2021). Discussions will include feminism, gender violence, migration, cultural commodification, economic and job insecurity, colonialism, and the effects of the 2008 global financial crisis. Readings of historical and theoretical texts will support the analysis of Bollaín’s works in class.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in HSPST or SPAIN at the 200 level or above, or consent of instructor.
Notes: Taught in Spanish.

TITLE: ANDEAN INDIGENEITY & MODERNIT
Course Name: Indigeneity and Modernity in the Andes
COMMENTS: Taught in Spanish.
Course Description: The cultural representations of religion, history, means of transportation, media, photography, etc., provide distinct points of view on how modernity has been perceived in the Andes. This course will introduce students to the recognition of those perspectives by looking closely at novels, short stories, and movies, produced from the 19th century to the present day. This course also will explore the diverse ways in which the intensification of modernity has changed the nature of Andean cultural production itself: its language, style, the narrator’s and characters’ worldviews, etc.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in HSPST or SPAIN at the 200 level or above, or consent of instructor.
Notes: Taught in Spanish

TITLE: SECOND TERM ITALIAN
Course Description: Continued study of speaking, writing, reading and listening comprehension. Highly interactive with a strong emphasis on obtaining both communicative and cultural competency in Italian. Classes supplemented by online vocabulary-building and grammar practice sessions and Language Center projects and activities. This course is only offered in the Spring.

TITLE: SECOND TERM ITALIAN
Course Description: Continued study of speaking, writing, reading and listening comprehension. Highly interactive with a strong emphasis on obtaining both communicative and cultural competency in Italian. Classes supplemented by online vocabulary-building and grammar practice sessions and Language Center projects and activities. This course is only offered in the Spring.

TITLE: FOURTH TERM ITALIAN
Course Description: Focus is on expanding vocabulary and strengthening verbal proficiency and writing skills through increased exposure to literary and cultural readings. This course is only offered in the Spring.

TITLE: HORROR, EXCESS, OBSCENITY
Course Name: Horror, Excess, Obscenity: Italy and its Specters
Course Description: Mainstream representations of Italian culture, art, and lifestyle often suggest that the country revolves around pleasure. Culinary richness, architectural wonders, passionate love, and lyrical masterpieces create an image of Italy that leaves little room for the menacing forces that still haunt it. By fully embracing a dialectical method that values contradictions and brings the repressed to the surface, this course explores what is horrific, excessive, and obscene in Italian culture. Through a theoretically informed inquiry, we will delve into the subsurface of deadly histories, censored literary objects, and extreme filmic experiments to examine not only the conditions that gave birth to them, but also the guises in which their specters continue to influence the present. By staring into the abyss of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, we will interrogate the politics of seeing what remains after catastrophe and whether aesthetic forms can—or cannot—represent the unthinkable. Myriads of old Gorgons await beneath the surface.
Notes: Warning: This course will analyze materials that some may find unsettling and/or deeply disturbing. Course taught in English; no previous knowledge of Italian required.

TITLE: STORIES OF TRAVELS & RETURNS
Course Name: Fuori di casa: Stories of Travels and Returns
Course Description: This course explores the concept of "being away from home" through various representations of travels and returns in Italian literature, cinema, music, and art. In these stories of movements and border-crossing, we will reflect on the idea of "home" with shifting social and cultural perspectives across time in Italian culture from Dante to Ferrante. In their shared themes of home and belonging, exile and border-crossing, these stories will guide us in understanding Italy and Italian as we know today, while helping us find home in a culture and in a language that is not our own.
Prerequisite Narrative: ITALN-200, ITALN-220, or approval of instructor.
Notes: Taught in Italian.

TITLE: SECOND TERM JAPANESE
Course Description: Continued work in speaking, listening, reading, and writing, with mastery of 99 kanji characters. Four 50-minute classes a week (Monday-Thursday).

TITLE: SECOND TERM JAPANESE
Course Description: Continued work in speaking, listening, reading, and writing, with mastery of 99 kanji characters. Four 50-minute classes a week (Monday-Thursday).

TITLE: FOURTH TERM JAPANESE
Course Description: Intermediate Japanese with continued emphasis on oral communication. An additional 108 kanji characters will be introduced. Four 50-minute classes a week (Monday-Thursday).

TITLE: TOPIC: JAPANESE LINGUISTICS
Course Description: This course explores Japanese phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax and semantics.  Students will compare Japanese with English and examine universal perspectives of language.

TITLE: JAPANESE SEMINAR
Course Name: Japanese Seminar: Advanced Writing and Research
Course Description: JAPN 500 develops the formal, discipline-specific writing skills required for advanced research and thesis work. Students compose analytical essays on topics in film studies, literature, or linguistics, with an emphasis on clarity, structure, and academic style.

TITLE: INTRODUCTION TO LAW
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Years.
Course Description: Focus on the American system of law: principally constitutional law, criminal law, and the development of civil rights. Topics include philosophical approaches to justice, English common law, and comparative analysis of French civil law and legal codes in socialist political systems and in majority Muslim countries. Consideration of the challenges to trust in legal institutions from the Supreme Court to local courts and police. Attention also to legal regimes regarding refugees, Native Americans, and defendants with mental illness.

TITLE: ANCIENT JEWISH WISDOM
Course Description: An introduction to the Jewish Tradition and Jewish way of reading.

TITLE: JEWISH FEMINISM
Course Description: This course examines the foundational texts, debates, and activism of Jewish feminism in the United States from the early 1970s to the present. Students will explore how Jewish women named and theorized gender inequality in Jewish law, ritual, theology, communal life, and cultural practice—and how those critiques reshaped American Judaism. Readings will situate Jewish feminist thought within wider developments in feminist, religious, and American social history. The course also considers LGBTQ Jewish ideas and activism, asking where they converge with, extend, or challenge Jewish feminist concerns. Students will gain a vocabulary for analyzing the movement’s central questions, historical evolution, and enduring impact on Jewish life today.

TITLE: AMERICAN JEWISH LITERATURE
Course Description: What makes a work “Jewish American literature”? Must it be written by a Jewish author, center Jewish characters or themes, or appear in a Jewish language? This course uses such questions to explore the American Jewish experience from the earliest Jewish settlement to the present, with particular attention to the period after 1865. Through fiction, poetry, memoir, drama, and other genres, students will examine how writers have represented migration, religion, family, race, belonging, assimilation, and cultural difference. Rather than imposing fixed definitions, the course treats “Jewish,” “American,” and “literature” as contested categories whose meanings have changed over time.

TITLE: ISRAEL THROUGH LIT AND FILM
Course Description: Analysis through Israeli Literature and Film of the internal and external conflicts that have shaped Israeli society since its founding as an independent state in 1948. The challenge of forging a national identity and identities out of diverse diasporas and cultures. Responses to repetitive trauma in an evolving Israeli identity. Readings and films engage students in moral, political, ideological and social debates and address the many sociopolitical, historical, and geographical conflicts of this small but ethnically, religiously, culturally and politically diverse society.

TITLE: BUILDING JERUSALEM
Course Name: Building Jerusalem: The Making and Remaking of a Holy City
Course Description: Since its foundation, the city of Jerusalem has been claimed materially and spiritually by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. This course will, through its art and architecture, trace the complex history of Jerusalem from ca. 957 BCE to today’s divided city. The art and architecture of the city is contextualized in a way that speaks beyond the often-used and simplistic tripartite manner of constructing identity and history in the city.

TITLE: ARABS & JEWS MIDDLE EAST
Course Name: Arabs and Jews in the Middle East
Course Description: Deep study of the Arab-Israeli conflict from the 1880s to the present. We will study the relations between Arab and Jewish communities, the roots of Zionism, Western imperialism, and Israeli and Palestinian social and political evolution.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any 200-level history course, GOVT-207, or permission of the instructor

TITLE: ELEMENTARY LATIN II
Course Description: Continuation of LATIN-110. Further study of grammar, syntax and vocabulary, accompanied by reading and discussion of passages that cast light on the society and culture of ancient Rome and its empire. For students who have completed LATIN-110 or those who have had some Latin but require review.
Notes: Three class meetings a week, in addition to a drill session. Language course not in English.

TITLE: THE ROMAN HERO
Course Description: Readings, in the original Latin, from Vergil’s Aeneid and other Roman epics. Consideration of the nature of heroism and epic poetry, with attention to the history, society and culture of the Roman world.

TITLE: RENAISSANCE OUTSIDERS
COMMENTS: Open to First Years only.
Course Description: From artists to utopian dreamers to iconoclastic peasants, the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries are teeming with marginalized people radically reimaging the terms of their own self-identity and rethinking the relationship between selfhood and the larger culture. As an interdisciplinary conversation, this course explores issues in literary, art and cultural history through the study of texts that expose and even help create a changing sense of selfhood in the early modern period.
Notes: (History or Intermedia)

TITLE: BLACK WOMEN'S LIT RENAISSANCE
COMMENTS: Open to First Years and Sophomores only. Students are restricted to one 100-level writing-intensive LIT course. 100-level LIT courses may not be taken after 200-level LIT courses.
Course Description: The twenty-year period between 1970 and 1990 is often referred to as the “Black Women’s Literary Renaissance” due to the unprecedented amount of literary and cultural production from black women in the United States. This course explores its profound contributions to black life and literature. Students will examine the intersections and oppositions among political movements, such as the Lesbian Feminist Movement and the Black Power Movement, and identify how these connections shaped the aesthetic landscape of the time. Course materials will include essays, novels, poems, and visual art, featuring Alice Walker, Toni Cade Bambara, bell hooks, Lorna Simpson, and others.
Notes: (Intermedia or Theory) (SSIH)

TITLE: LIT: WHAT IS IT GOOD FOR?
Course Name: Literature: What Is It Good For?
COMMENTS: Open to First-Years Only (FYC). Students are restricted to one 100-level writing-intensive LIT course. 100-level LIT courses may not be taken after 200-level LIT courses.
Course Description: Debates about the value of literature have long been tied to questions about its use. Literature has been praised—and condemned—as a source of pleasure, a medium for the transmission of knowledge, and a vehicle of personal expression. In order to determine why fiction matters, we will examine works that explore the power of literature to shape moral, social, and political realities, including philosophical manifestos, anti-slavery treatises, self-help manuals, and experimental novels. Works by Rousseau, Cugoano, Wollstonecraft, and George Eliot, as well as the film The Servant (1963).
Notes: (Genre or Theory)

TITLE: REWRITING POCAHONTAS
Course Description: Who was Pocahontas, and why are Americans still so obsessed with her? Where does Pocahontas the historical person end, and Pocahontas-the-myth begin? And how have Indigenous writers and scholars rewritten and rethought the Pocahontas narrative? In this course we will trace the historical development of “Pocahontas” across genres and media. Texts will include histories (John Smith’s Generall Historie), dramas (The Indian Princess, the first American play about American Indians), poems (Lydia Sigourney’s epic poem Pocahontas) and films (Disney’s Pocahontas and Malik’s The New World). We will read these settler-authored texts in conversation with Indigenous-authored accounts of the historical Pocahontas (Powhatan name Matoaka) and the Indian princess trope.
Notes: (History or Intermedia) (SSIH)

TITLE: POETRY & POETICS
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. Not open to senior English or Creative Writing concentrators.
Course Description: This course examines how poems work: how they are constructed, and how they produce meaning, pleasure, and cultural value. We will study poetry in terms of prosody, conventions, history, genre, and reception, with the goal of teaching the essential skills of close reading and contextual interpretation. Readings are primarily from the traditions of poetry written in English.
Prerequisite Narrative: For first-years, one course in literature or a 4 or 5 on AP LIT or LANG. No prerequisite for upperclass students.
Notes: (Genre or History) Not open to senior English or Creative Writing concentrators.

TITLE: GENDER&VIOLENCE MIDDLE AGES
Course Name: Gender and Violence in the Middle Ages
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: This course serves as an introduction to the field of Medieval and Renaissance Studies. Drawing on multiple disciplinary perspectives, including those of literature, law, history, and art, we will examine the intersection of ideas about the body, gender, and violence in the European Middle Ages. Readings may include the Bible and early patristic writings; the lives of saints; poems and advice manuals on courtly love; depictions of women in the Crusades; Icelandic sagas; and perspectives on the trial of Joan of Arc.
Prerequisite Narrative: One 100-level course in Literature or History or AP 4 or 5 in English or History
Notes: (History)

TITLE: BOLLYWOOD FILM
Course Description: The course charts a history of Bollywood, India’s mainstream Hindi-language film industry. Although dismissed for its use of melodrama and song-dance sequences, Bollywood has long engaged with other global cinemas and critiqued social, cultural, and political trends. Readings and films span romances about gender and nation like Mother India (1957) and Chaudhvin Ka Chand (1960); the 1970s "angry young man" oeuvre and its later avatars, crime and terrorist films; diasporic family dramas like Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003); and crossover hits like The Lunch Box (2013) that address the globalized present.
Notes: (Genre or History) This course may be offered as writing-intensive or not writing-intensive, per the deparment. Refer to the schedule for details.

TITLE: TONI MORRISON
Course Description: This course is an in-depth study of Toni Morrison’s fictional works and critical writing. Students will explore her creative and scholarly contributions to ideas of community and genealogy, as well as to representations of race, gender, and nation. Students will also explore her attention to language, form, and literary theory. In studying both Morrison’s formal and theoretical commitments, students will develop an awareness of how literature serves as a vehicle for animating and critiquing social, historical, and ethical concerns in our world. Assignments will include short critical essays, collaborative presentations and projects, and readings will include "The Source of Self-Regard," "The Bluest Eye," "Song of Solomon," and "Jazz."
Notes: (Theory or Genre)

TITLE: FILMS OF THE COEN BROTHERS
Course Name: The Films of the Coen Brothers: Genre and Pastiche at the end of the American Mythos
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
Course Description: This course will analyze the way the Coen Brothers’ films play with previously hegemonic myths about the American experience. How do their films negotiate expectations of genre? What happens to meaning when pastiche or appropriation become vital to the narrative and imaginary world of the films? We will watch up to a dozen films, including Fargo, No Country for Old Men, Miller’s Crossing, O Brother Where art Thou and The Big Lebowski, not quite in chronological order,. Readings from scholarly and theoretical material, as well as excerpts from many of their sources, from Homer to Hammett. We'll also consider some of the 20th century painting, architecture and style that informs their films. Mandatory out of class viewings.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Literature or Cinema and Media Studies, or permission of instructor
Notes: (Intermedia or Theory)

TITLE: RECONSTITUTING CONSTITUTION
COMMENTS: Open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
Course Description: This course explores the “Constitutional Moment” as a broad sociocultural formation in the decades just before and after the turn of the nineteenth century, and as a recurring American phenomenon thereafter. We will begin by analyzing the founding documents as rhetorical performances, reading the aspirations and anxieties they express in relation to those legible in contemporaneous literary texts. Then we’ll turn to political, literary, and cinematic works across subsequent American generations that figuratively re-stage the founding moment even as they radically re-frame its stakes and stakeholders. Likely authors: A. Hamilton, T. Jefferson, W. Irving, H.D. Thoreau, F. Douglass, E.C. Stanton, W. Whitman, A. Lincoln, G. Stein, R. Ellison, G. Lucas, L.M. Miranda.
Notes: (History)

TITLE: AMERICAN LIT 19TH CENTURY
Course Description: A lot happened in this country in the nineteenth century. Slavery was expanded and then eventually abolished. Women fought for equal rights and didn't get them. Indigenous peoples were attacked and displaced – but refused to vanish. Waves of immigrants arrived and dispersed. There was a civil war. Meanwhile, the novel became a mass-market media sensation. Poetry was a set of popular genres that everyone read. Melodramas attracted large crowds. New versions of American philosophy rose and fell. People tried to write their life stories. In this course we will read some of those novels, poems, autobiographies, and philosophical essays (by Stowe, Wheatley, Douglass, Thoreau, and Whitman, among others) against the historical backdrop of war, immigration, forced removal, misogyny, and racism.
Notes: (Genre or History)

TITLE: SIBERIAN TEXT
Course Description: This course is an exploration of five centuries of writing in and about Siberia. While we will root ourselves in the socio-historical context, our main goal is to engage meaningfully with the very process of the formation of the Siberian Text. By this, scholars of the region mean the body of works that emerged out of the geographical, political, anthropological, and cultural categorizations of Siberia. The plurality of voices and the diversity of spatial experiences engaged in the process of creating the Siberian Text include travelers, criminals, political prisoners, religious dissenters, shamans, hunters, ethnographers, missionaries, vagabonds, and peasants. Probing the fraught legacy of the current spatial discourse on Siberia, the course will examine a variety of media and genres, including official documents, travelogues, oral tradition(s), works of fiction, autobiographies, pictorial art, and film. In addition to the transnational and transhistorical dimensions, we will engage with theories of space and place, imagined geographies, and ecocriticism.

TITLE: AMERICAN JEWISH LITERATURE
Course Description: What makes a work “Jewish American literature”? Must it be written by a Jewish author, center Jewish characters or themes, or appear in a Jewish language? This course uses such questions to explore the American Jewish experience from the earliest Jewish settlement to the present, with particular attention to the period after 1865. Through fiction, poetry, memoir, drama, and other genres, students will examine how writers have represented migration, religion, family, race, belonging, assimilation, and cultural difference. Rather than imposing fixed definitions, the course treats “Jewish,” “American,” and “literature” as contested categories whose meanings have changed over time.

TITLE: VIDEO ESSAYS
Course Name: Video Essays: Writing with Sound and Image
COMMENTS: 0.5 credit course; Meets 1/20/27-3/12/27.
Course Description: Videographic criticism is a multimodal form of writing. In using sound and image to comment on audiovisual texts, the video essay blurs the line between object and method of study. This hands-on humanities lab introduces students to a wide range of videographic techniques and formats, and some of the theoretical and philosophical concerns driving recent developments in the field. Students learn to not only craft their own video essays, but display greater reflexivity about their aesthetic choices, interventions and compositional process. No prior editing or other digital experience required.
Notes: Open to Sophomores, Juniors, and Seniors.

TITLE: AVANT GARDE CINEMA
Course Name: Avant Garde: Cinema as Theory and Critique
Course Description: A history of alternatives to commercial movies, focusing on surrealist and dadaist film, visual music, psychodrama, direct cinema, the film society movement,  personal cinema, the New American Cinema, structuralism, Queer cinema, feminist cinema, minor cinema, recycled cinema and devotional cinema.  While conventional entertainment films use the novel, the short story and the stage drama as their primary instigations, experimental and avant-garde films are analogous to music, poetry, painting, sculpture and collage.
Notes: Not open to first-year students.

TITLE: 'EARING ACCENT (METHODS)
Course Description: Everyone speaks with an accent. But where some people's speech is deemed "neutral," others are cast as "accented." Racialized and classed perceptions about language and fluency infuse literature as well as the realms of education, housing, employment, and immigration. How might we reframe "accent" such that it unsettles assumptions about linguistic identity and cultural worth? To what extent are accents visual, aural, and textual, not just oral? Course texts may include: My Fair Lady; Sorry to Bother You; episodes from The Simpsons and Modern Family; creative non-fiction, fiction, and poetry.
Prerequisite Narrative: A 200-level course in Literature, Africana Studies, or Women's and Gender Studies
Notes: (Intermedia) (Methods)

TITLE: SHAKESPEARE AND APPROPRIATION
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores.
Course Description: This class focuses on appropriation as a central condition for considering Shakespeare's drama. Along with plays by Shakespeare we will study how his plays have been appropriated by others. In addition, we will investigate how Shakespeare considered appropriation and adaptation a prime method of literary production by studying contemporary plays, ancient literature and a diversity other sources that Shakespeare likely considered in his own composition process. In so doing we will see the exchanges and vital engagement Shakespeare shows with his own reading.
Notes: (Genre or History)

TITLE: ORIGINS OF THE NOW
Course Name: Origins of the Now: Transatlantic Modernism--Methods
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., and Sophomores.
Course Description: This course explores the origin stories of several literary and cultural forms that we now take for granted, including free verse, film, the literary magazine, and stream-of-consciousness narration. To do so, we will look at how early 20th century American and British writers and artists worked to reconceive foundational notions such as class, race, gender, self, sex, and time in response to the collapse of traditional Victorian values. Readings and viewings include works by Chaplin, Eliot, H.D., Griffith, Hughes, Joyce, Larsen, Loy, Pound, Toomer, Woolf and other possibilities. Attention given to the various scholarly methods for studying this rich and diverse literature.
Notes: (Methods)

TITLE: WOMEN & THE ENLIGHTENMENT
Course Description: This course explores women’s relation to the intellectual and political culture of Enlightenment Britain. We will study how warring ideas about the rights of man shaped conceptions and representations of sexual difference and womanhood over the course of the long eighteenth century. Treating "woman" as a historical category will, in turn, help us to better understand the underlying assumptions and consequences of our own thinking about gender. Primary texts by Mary Astell, Mary Wollstonecraft, Austen, and Mme de Stael. Feminist scholarship by Nancy K. Miller, Nancy Armstrong, and Toril Moi.
Notes: (History or Theory)

TITLE: RACE & NATION MIDDLE AGES
Course Name: Race and Nation in the Middle Ages
Course Description: What did race and nation mean in the Middle Ages? We’ll first examine English attempts to establish a unified national identity out of a history of invasion and colonization. We’ll consider the role of Jews in England, as well as examples of Celtic resistance to English imperialism. Then we’ll turn to writing that explores English identity in an international context, to see how real and imagined contact with other cultures—particularly during the Crusades—influences conceptions of nation, race, and identity. Genres include travel writing, drama, romance, and historical narrative.
Notes: (History)

TITLE: SEM FAULKNER & THE SOUTH
Course Description: Faulkner’s major novels, published between the late 1920s and the early 1940s, trace his most impassioned struggle with the legacies of slavery, the enduring hierarchies of gender and class, and the rising specter of industrialization’s destructive force. We’ll explore the series of radical formal innovations Faulkner arrived at in order to convey these stories, and to convey the inextricability of one from the next—both in American society and in individual consciousness. Readings: Light in August, Absalom, Absalom, Go Down, Moses, and more.
Notes: (Genre or History)

TITLE: SEM: INDEPENDENT PROJECTS
COMMENTS: Instructor's Signature Req.
Course Description: In this seminar, students will pursue independent research projects culminating in a longer paper (25-35 pages) on a topic of their choosing. Seminar sessions will discuss strategies for organizing and drafting a longer paper, time management, the best ways to use research tools, and different ideas about how to revise; later there will be opportunities to share drafts and address issues that arise.
Notes: Graded Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory

TITLE: LATIN AMERICAN MUSIC
Course Description: Through the lens of musicology and ethnomusicology, this course explores folk/vernacular, popular, and classical music from various Latin American locales and Latino societies in the U.S. Lessons and readings include genres, instruments, and performance practices as well as contextualization with history, politics, and entertainment. Course also interrogates what defines Latin American and Latino musical identities. The course includes in-class, hands-on performances. No ability to read music is required.

TITLE: INTRO U.S. LATINX/LIT
Course Description: Examines cultural production of representative U.S. Latinx writers primarily from the civil rights movement to present. The course explores Latinx writers’ engagement with language, political status, race, gender, nationality, and generational markers to reveal both the fluidity and instability of the Latinx imaginary. Readings include autobiographical and biographical works, bildungsroman, memoir, historical novel and vignettes in an exploration of the self and one’s relation to collective identity.
Notes: Taught in English. Not open to seniors.

TITLE: LATIN AMERICAN MUSIC
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Sophomores, & 1st Yrs. Open to Music majors/minors only or instructor permission.
Course Description: Through the lens of musicology and ethnomusicology, this course explores folk/vernacular, popular, and classical music from various Latin American locales and Latino societies in the U.S. Lessons and readings include genres, instruments, and performance practices as well as contextualization with history, politics, and entertainment. Course also interrogates what defines Latin American and Latino musical identities. The course includes in-class, hands-on performances. No ability to read music is required.

TITLE: WONDER & CERTAINTY
Course Name: Wonder and Certainty in Science and Religion
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: Are we the only rational beings in the universe? Is such a thing as a soul? Can we predict the future? The truism goes that history is told by the victors, and the same is true for the history of ideas -- so, join us for a journey into the history of ideas that haven't made it into modern textbooks. Featuring materials from Hamilton College’s Special Collections, this course focuses on a series of case studies from early modern Europe and the Atlantic world that represent pivot points to teleologies in the history of science and thought. The result is a history of wonderment followed by doubt, illuminating divergent and sometimes abandoned paths once frequented by the wisest among humankind.

TITLE: CALCULUS I
Course Description: Introduction to the differential and integral calculus of a single variable. Topics include limits, continuity, derivatives, max-min problems and integrals. For students matriculating in 2013 or later, this course may not be counted toward the concentration or minor.
Notes: Four hours of class.

TITLE: CALCULUS II
Course Description: 116 F,S Calculus II – A continuation of the study begun in 113. Methods of integration, improper integrals, applications of integration to volume and arc length, parametric equations, sequences and series, power series, vectors, and an introduction to 3-dimensional coordinate systems with equations of lines and planes. Prerequisite, 113 or placement by the department. The Department.
Notes: Completion of 116 with a grade of C- or greater gives Hamilton credit for both 113 and 116 for those students placed into 116.

COMMENTS: Not open to students who have taken ECON 166, ECON 265 or MATH 252.
Course Description: An introduction to the principles and methods of applied statistics. Topics include exploratory data analysis, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, analysis of variance and categorical data analysis. Extensive reliance on statistical computer software and authentic data.
Notes: May not be taken by students who have taken or are taking ECON-166, ECON-265, PSYCH-201, NEURO-201 or GOVT-230.

Course Description: Introduction to functions of more than one variable, partial derivatives, multiple integrals in two and three dimensions, line and surface integrals, Green’s Theorem, curl, divergence, the Divergence Theorem and Stokes’ Theorem. Course Description: Theory and applications of differential equations, including first-order equations, second-order linear equations, systems of equations, and qualitative and numerical methods.

COMMENTS: Not Open to Those Who Took Econ 400 Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: A second course in introductory statistics with a focus on applications to real data using the statistical software R. Topics include linear and logistic regression, analysis of variance, categorical data analysis, and selected topics in randomization and machine learning. Emphasis will be placed on interpretation and presentation of results. Depending on the topic  chosen by the student for their final project, with the permission of the instructor, may count toward the Social, Structural, and Institutional Hierarchies requirement.
Notes: Students who have a score of 4 or 5 in AP Statistics may enroll with the instructor's permission. May not be taken by students who have taken or are taking Econ 400.

TITLE: DECISIONS & APPLIED MATH
Course Name: Decisions by Design: Applied Mathematics in Society
Course Description: This course introduces applied mathematics in various social contexts with an emphasis on communication to non-experts. Its focus is exploring how mathematical tools such as calculus, linear algebra, optimization, and algorithms help shape decision-making in real-world applications. Depending on instructor expertise and student interest, applications may include search algorithms, apportionment methods, resource allocation, political districting, and more. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with mathematical skills to analyze complex systems and think critically about how to deploy mathematics to solve real-world problems.

TITLE: REAL ANALYSIS
Course Description: An introduction to analysis. Topics include completeness of the real numbers, cardinality, sequences, series, real-valued functions of a real variable, limits, and continuity.

TITLE: COMPLEX ANALYSIS
Course Description: An introduction to the theory of analytic functions of a complex variable: Cauchy-Riemann equations, contour integration, Cauchy-Goursat theorem, Liouville theorem, Taylor and Laurent expansions, Residue theory.

TITLE: GRAPH THEORY
Course Description: An introduction to the theory and applications of graph theory. Topics include: trees; connectivity; Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs; vertex-, edge- and map-colorings; digraphs; tournaments; matching theory; planarity and Ramsey numbers.

TITLE: MODERN ALGEBRA
Course Description: An introduction to the three fundamental structures of abstract algebra: groups, rings and fields.

TITLE: PROB & STAT INFERENCE
Course Description: An introduction to set-theoretic probability with applications to mathematical statistics. Topics include probability spaces, discrete and continuous random variables, single and multivariate distributions, and limit theorems, leading into the mathematical theory of estimators, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-216 and an introductory statistics course which may be one of the following: MATH-152, ECON-166, PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201, or GOVT-230. Students who have a score of 4 or 5 in AP Statistics may enroll with the instructor’s permission.
Prerequisites: MATH 216, , MATH-152, , ECON-166, , PSYCH-201, , NEURO-201, , GOVT-230,

TITLE: STAT METHODS MACHINE LEARNING
Course Description: This course covers statistical methods in machine learning such as decision trees, random forests and support vector machines The course will use a project-based approach to give students hands-on experience using these techniques by analyzing large and complex real-world datasets. More importantly, they will learn the statistical principles behind these procedures, such as loss functions, maximum likelihood estimation and bias-variance trade-off as well as why these principles matter in real world settings.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-254 or, with permission of the instructor,  MATH-351 plus programming experience.

TITLE: GROUP THEORY
Course Description: This course is an introduction to groups, one of the fundamental structures of abstract algebra. The course builds on concepts introduced in Math 325. Group theory is used in many areas of mathematics and other STEM fields. This course will explore the basic structures and properties of groups as well as some basic operations on groups. The theory will be introduced and illustrated through classic examples. Applications of groups will also be discussed.

TITLE: MEDIEVAL CHRISTIANITIES
Course Description: A survey of the development of the Christian religion in premodern Eurasia and the Mediterranean, from its elevation to a state cult in the later Roman Empire to about 1450. Special consideration will be given to the growth of the church and processes of conversion, the problem of authority versus heresy and heterodoxy, and the relationship of the Christian churches to Islam and other non-Christian peoples. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.

TITLE: GENDER&VIOLENCE MIDDLE AGES
Course Name: Gender and Violence in the Middle Ages
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only.
Course Description: This course serves as an introduction to the field of Medieval and Renaissance Studies. Drawing on multiple disciplinary perspectives, including those of literature, law, history, and art, we will examine the intersection of ideas about the body, gender, and violence in the European Middle Ages. Readings may include the Bible and early patristic writings; the lives of saints; poems and advice manuals on courtly love; depictions of women in the Crusades; Icelandic sagas; and perspectives on the trial of Joan of Arc.
Prerequisite Narrative: One 100-level course in Literature (LIT) or History (HIST), or AP 4 or 5 in English or History
Notes: (History)

TITLE: NORTHERN RENAISSANCE ART
Course Description: This course explores the distinctive ways in which art was crafted and consumed in northern Europe during the age of Renaissance and Reformation. We will examine paintings and prints, propaganda and princely splendor, and carved altarpieces and ceremonial armor against the backdrop of both city and court, while considering issues of religious function, social use, and the economic history of the arts. The course also fosters a critical awareness of the methods of art history by drawing attention to scholarship on Northern art that has, in many ways, laid the foundations for modernity.

TITLE: GUNPOWDER ISLAM
Course Name: Gunpowder Islam: Empires in Turkey, Iran, and India, c.1500-1800
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Fifty years ago, the scholar Marshall Hodgson coined the term "gunpowder empires" to describe the introduction of new military technology by early modern Islamic kingdoms across Eurasia, specifically in Turkey, Iran, and India. Using this cultural framework to study the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal Empires, this course will focus on issues of imperial power and expansion, social and religious authority, protest and dissent, language and literature, law and ethics, paintings and architecture, as well as gender and sexuality. We will explore the historiography of these Islamic polities along with reading primary sources including court chronicles, local histories, political treatises, religious texts, and poetry in Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit, Hindavi and other languages.

Course Name: Wonder and Certainty in Science and Religion
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: Are we the only rational beings in the universe? Is such a thing as a soul? Can we predict the future? The truism goes that history is told by the victors, and the same is true for the history of ideas -- so, join us for a journey into the history of ideas that haven't made it into modern textbooks. Featuring materials from Hamilton College’s Special Collections, this course focuses on a series of case studies from early modern Europe and the Atlantic world that represent pivot points to teleologies in the history of science and thought. The result is a history of wonderment followed by doubt, illuminating divergent and sometimes abandoned paths once frequented by the wisest among humankind.

TITLE: MADNESS, LOVESICKNESS, & JINN
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. First Years require instructor permission.
Course Description: “Madness” evokes images of rambling, potentially violent, individuals on the margins of society. How did historical attitudes to insanity evolve in early modern and modern Eurasia? Were madpeople always ostracized or were they simply objects of sympathy and pity? What did hospitals and other networks of care and healing look like for mentally ill patients? In poetry, the pain of separation of the lover from their beloved produced lovesickness. Finally, demonic possession of the brain by jinns (Islamic spirits) was thought to cause madness. How can we understand the literary, religious and supernatural world of these actors without dismissing it? This course will take a holistic view of insanity while engaging with the rise of asylums or other lunatic institutions.

TITLE: MINORITIES IN THE MIDDLE EAST
Course Name: Minorities in the Middle East: History, Religion, and Relations with Political Powers
Course Description: This course explores how minority communities in the Middle East—Druze, ʿAlawites, Kurds, Yezidis, Armenians, Maronites, Copts, Assyrians, and others—have been formed and transformed from the late Ottoman era to the present. Beginning with the shift from imperial pluralism to nation-state “minorities,” it examines how religion, identity, nationalism, and political power shape communal identity and minority–state relations. Case studies span Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, addressing genocide, displacement, nationalism, citizenship, security, and diaspora. Drawing on history, anthropology, religious studies, and political science, students examine how communities negotiate identity, power, and recognition in a plural Middle East. This course examines historical and contemporary experiences of minority communities in the Middle East. Some course materials address difficult subjects, including genocide, mass violence, persecution, forced displacement, sexual violence, religious and ethnic discrimination, and war. These topics are approached in their historical and scholarly contexts and are essential to understanding the experiences of the communities studied in the course.

TITLE: RESISTANCE HISTORY THRU FILM
Course Name: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

Course Name: Building Jerusalem: The Making and Remaking of a Holy City
Course Description: Since its foundation, the city of Jerusalem has been claimed materially and spiritually by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. This course will, through its art and architecture, trace the complex history of Jerusalem from ca. 957 BCE to today’s divided city. The art and architecture of the city is contextualized in a way that speaks beyond the often-used and simplistic tripartite manner of constructing identity and history in the city.

TITLE: POSTCOL THEORY & ISLAMIC ART
Course Description: How does the study of art and architectural history interface with colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial structures of power? This is a pressing question for those who study the visual cultures of the Middle East, a region in which these power structures have had considerable impact historically as well as in the contemporary moment. This class will consider from theoretical and practical vantage points how colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial systems and institutions have governed or influenced the methods of study, scope, and modes of display of historical art from the Middle East. Topics will include colonial-era collection and museum practices, Orientalism and its critics, post-colonial nationalist art historical discourses, cultural heritage in and during the ‘wars on terror’, and visual discourses of contemporary Islamophobia. Students may pursue research projects with objects or items from the Wellin Museum and/or the Michael Lang ’67 Special Collections and Archives.

Topics range from reading notes and rhythms to analyzing and formulating chord progressions. Study of basic musical structures of the Western classical tonal idiom ("classical" music) and contemporary popular music practices that have developed from that. No previous knowledge of music required.

TITLE: INTRO TO MEDIA:INTEGRATED MED
Course Name: Introduction to Media: Integrated Media and Emerging Practices
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph, Jrs, and Srs.
Course Description: This course will serve as an introduction to digital technology in contemporary art making as it relates to interactivity, collaboration, and emerging practices.  Emphasis will be placed on hands on experimentation and exploration across disciplines. We will cover installation art, web art, digital and time-based art, and immersive environments. Students will gain an overview of emerging digital practices, collaborative production strategies and correlations to social, aesthetic and theoretical issues. Other topics may include virtuality, performance, cyborgs, and network culture.

TITLE: ROOTS TO COUNTRY MUSIC
Course Name: Roots Music to Country Music: The Making of an American Sound
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: Study of country music from its roots in cowboy songs, fiddle tunes, blues, bluegrass, and gospel hymns to current artists like The [Dixie] Chicks, Taylor Swift, and Brad Paisley. Artists include the Carter Family, Hank Williams, Patsy Cline, Dolly Parton, Willie Nelson, Emmylou Harris, Lynyrd Skynyrd, & Garth Brooks. Study of the musical elements, social class, gender roles, and cultural contexts of styles such as Western Swing, Honky-Tonk, Rockabilly, the Nashville Sound, Southern Rock, and Alt-country. Includes films such as Coal Miner's Daughter, Nashville, and O Brother, Where Art Thou?
Notes: No previous knowledge of music required. Music concentrators and minors are strongly encouraged to register for MUSIC-217. MUSIC-217 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 200-level only with instructor’s permission.

TITLE: LATIN AMERICAN MUSIC
Course Description: Through the lens of musicology and ethnomusicology, this course explores folk/vernacular, popular, and classical music from various Latin American locales and Latino societies in the U.S. Lessons and readings include genres, instruments, and performance practices as well as contextualization with history, politics, and entertainment. Course also interrogates what defines Latin American and Latino musical identities. The course includes in-class, hands-on performances. No ability to read music is required.

TITLE: FROM BACH TO BARTOK
Course Description: Instrumental music from the eighteenth, nineteenth, and first half of the twentieth centuries with an emphasis on orchestral works by composers such as Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms, Mahler, Debussy, Stravinsky, and Bartók. Attention also given to piano and chamber works, including music by women composers. Consideration of the history and development of musical instruments and the use of instrumental classical music in popular culture (as in the films Apocalypse Now, The Shining, 2001: A Space Odyssey, Platoon).
Prerequisite Narrative: MUSIC-100, MUSIC-110, MUSIC-210, MUSIC-211, MUSIC-220, MUSIC-141/142, or consent of instructor
Prerequisites: MUSIC 100, , MUSIC-110, , MUSIC-210, , MUSIC-211, , MUSIC-220, , MUSIC-141/142,

TITLE: INTERMED MEDIA: NEW FRONTIERS
Course Name: Intermediate Media: New Frontiers in Storytelling
COMMENTS: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab.
Course Description: This class will survey and create emergent and non -linear forms of storytelling using digital and hybrid tools. We will examine notions of narrative authority and hybridity in a digital age and think through different ways we might use technology to distill, break apart or reify modes of communication and visual metaphor. Discussion will push boundaries of traditional storytelling and consider connectivity, liveness and embodied presence. This course will draw on multiple forms of expression including but not limited to digital media, performance, sound, XR, web, and network environments.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any intro-level Digital Arts studio course, including cross-listed.
Prerequisites: ART-113, , DARTS-113, , MUSIC-113, , ART 116, , DARTS-212, , ART-213, , DARTS-213, , ART-221, , DARTS-221, , MUSIC-270,

TITLE: ADV. GROUP PERFORMANCE
Course Description: The study of music through chamber performance in one or more of the following: Instrumental Chamber Ensembles (Buchman), Hamilton Voices (Botha), Jazz Combo (Woods). Co-requisite, concurrent registration in the corresponding Group Performance ensemble required (i.e., Orchestra, College Choir or Jazz Ensemble respectively, and consent of instructor).
Notes: One-quarter course credit each semester. May be repeated. Students may count up to four credits from among MUSIC-141, MUSIC-142, MUSIC-241, and MUSIC-242 toward graduation.

TITLE: MUSIC IN AMER FILM
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Years.
Course Description: Examination of music in American film from silent films to the present with emphasis on the golden age of Hollywood. Topics include the development of musical conventions in film, different approaches of film composers (Steiner, Tiomkin, Rózsa, Herrmann, Newman, Bernstein, Williams), the meanings that music brings to film narratives. Includes films such as Casablanca, The Adventures of Robin Hood, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, A Streetcar Named Desire, Amadeus, The Shawshank Redemption, Oh Brother, Where Art Thou? Special attention to Hitchcock films (Psycho, Vertigo, Rear Window).
Prerequisite Narrative: Two courses, in any combination, in MUSIC, Cinema and Media Studies (CNMS), or Literature (LIT)
Notes: Three hours per week for film viewings in addition to class time. Music 345 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor’s permission.

TITLE: JAZZ CONNECTIONS
Course Description: An advanced jazz course that builds on the topics covered in Jazz Foundations (MUSIC 161), and examines the construction of the “jazz tradition” from a historiographical perspective. Considers how the development of jazz, and its construction in the context of educational institutions, both reflects and shapes concepts of race and gender in American culture. Includes an examination of the impact of jazz genres including hip hop, R&B, and gospel, and focuses on the international proliferation of jazz.
Prerequisite Narrative: MUSIC 161/261, AFRST 161/261, MUSIC 257/357, AFRST 257/357, or consent instructor
Notes: Not open to students who have taken MUSIC/AFRST 259/359. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor's permission.

TITLE: INTRO MUSIC, SOUND & TECH
Course Name: Introduction to Music, Sound, and Technology
Course Description: An introduction to the essential tools of 21st-century musicians, with an emphasis on creative practice and critical reflection. Students will learn to record, edit, process, and synthesize sound digitally; produce music using MIDI keyboards and software instruments; distribute their work; and critically engage with topics linked to the emergence of digital audio technologies. Listening and reading will include a wide range of works by Halim El-Dabh, Karlheinz Stockhausen, Pauline Oliveros, Pamela Z, and others. Open to all students regardless of musical background; additional resources for relevant music theory will be provided.

TITLE: INTERMEDIATE AURAL SKILLS
COMMENTS: Instructor's Signature Required. See professor for specific meeting day/time information.
Course Description: A continuation of 180. Development of aural understanding through sight-singing and dictation.  Tonic and dominant arpeggiation in inversion, diatonic melodies with simple modulation, further work in minor keys, introduction to alto and tenor clefs, chromatic intervals, harmonic progressions, rhythms in mixed meters, modal scales. May be repeated for credit with the consent of instructor. One-half course credit.

TITLE: ADV TOPICS MUSIC THEORY
Course Description: Intensive study of music theory topics, analytical techniques, and compositional approaches applied to common musical forms and styles from different traditions, including Western classical music, popular, jazz, film, theater, and selected world music. Selected repertoire will emphasize 20th- and 21st-century practices.

Course Description: The study of music through lessons in voice, flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, saxophone, horn, trumpet, trombone, euphonium, tuba, piano, organ, harp, percussion, classical guitar, jazz/contemporary guitar, folk guitar, violin, viola, cello, and contrabass. Notes: Students may only enroll in Advanced Solo Performance upon completion of or co-registration in MUSIC-110, MUSIC-210, or MUSIC-211. May be repeated for credit. A fee is charged.

Course Description: This course will explore the techniques of audio production in the recording studio and the increasingly portable platforms for computer music that continue to be developed. Topics will include digital audio synthesis, digital signal processing, MIDI and other systems for controlling audio, mixing, and mastering. Students will work in digital audio workstations and music programming environments. Projects will include producing a professional-quality album of music.
