COMMENTS: Instructor's Signature Required. See the MUSIC department for more information.
Course Description: A continuation of 281. May include continued work in alto and tenor clef, reading open scores, more advanced figured harmony and advanced sight-reading.  One-half course credit. May be repeated for credit.

TITLE: STATS & RESEARCH METHODS
Course Name: Statistics and Research Methods in Psychology
Course Description: The application and interpretation of descriptive and inferential statistics in the study of psychological processes. Some instruction in research design and methodological issues. Students will learn to use the statistical computer program SPSS to analyze data. Topics include the principles of hypothesis testing, t tests, analysis of variance, regression, and some non-parametric statistics.

TITLE: HUMAN NEUROSCIENCE
Course Description: Introduction to the field of neuroscience from a behavioral and cognitive perspective. Survey of experimental and clinical research involving humans and non-human animals, addressing presumed neural mechanisms for cognitive, motivational and emotional states. Analysis of amnesia, aphasia, agnosias, apraxias and disconnection syndromes.

TITLE: GENES, MOLECULES, & CELLS
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores only. Not open to those who took BIO 248.
Course Description: An intermediate course that examines genetics and biochemistry within the context of the cell. This course will focus on the macromolecules of life, genetic material and classical genetics, fundamental biochemical pathways, and cellular structure and function. A particular focus will be placed on proteins and nucleic acids and how cells use these molecules to direct the mechanisms of inheritance, energy production, and cellular reproduction. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisites: BIO-100A, , BIO-100B, , BIO-100D, , BIO-100E, , BIO-100F, , BIO-100G, , BIO-100H, , BIO 100I, , BIO-100J, , BIO-100K,
Usual instructor: Natalie Nannas, Noelle Relles, Wei-Jen Chang, Rhea Datta
Notes: Freshman and sophomores only; juniors and seniors will need permission of instructor.

TITLE: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE
Course Description: Dementia involves progressive loss of cognitive functions, associated with unique patterns of neurodegeneration in the brain. For example, Alzheimer’s disease is associated with memory loss and temporal lobe atrophy, whereas frontotemporal dementia is characterized by behavioral changes associated with frontal lobe atrophy. This course will discuss the different etiologies of dementia, the biological changes associated with different subtypes, risk factors (behavioral, genetic, etc.), neuropsychological and imaging-based methods for diagnosis, current treatment options, and the emotional, social, and economic costs of dementia on patients and caregivers. We will delve into primary scientific literature covering current theories and findings, and will explore cultural depictions to better understand dementia from multiple viewpoints. This course has substantial neurobiology content and students are required to have completed Fundamentals of Neurobiology (Neuro 205) to enroll.

TITLE: STRESS & PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGY
Course Description: A theoretical and methodological exploration of the psychological and physiological mechanisms of stress. Questions will include: How does psychological stress impact health and well-being? What neurobiological mechanisms are involved? What is the role of environmental context? Laboratory exercises will include designing original experiments to examine the role of stress on behavior and physiological activity, as well as analyzing data, writing papers based on findings, and oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology. (Same as PSYCH/NEURO-329.)

TITLE: SYSTEMS NEUROSCIENCE
Course Description: The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.

COMMENTS: Open to First Years Only.
Course Description: An introduction to various theories and expressions of 19th and 20th century existential thought.  Readings include Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Camus, Heidegger, Sartre, Wright, and de Beauvoir.

COMMENTS: Open to Sophomores and Juniors Only.

TITLE: INTRO POLITICAL THEORY
Course Description: Survey of selected political theorists from Plato to the present. Examination of questions of liberty, equality, justice and community.
Notes: Open to juniors and seniors with consent of instructor only. Offered as Proseminar & Writing-Intensive at least once per year. (Political Theory)

Notes: Open to juniors and seniors with consent of instructor only. Offered as Proseminar & Writing-Intensive at least once per year. (Political Theory)

TITLE: PHIL PERSPECTIVE SELF
COMMENTS: Open to First Years and Sophomores only.
Course Description: What is a self?  Does each person have one?  Does each person have only one? How is the self related to the soul?  Is it unchanging or in constant flux? What is the relationship between the self and the body?  Examination of personal identity, the self and the soul as these topics are addressed in traditional philosophical texts, literature and the natural and behavioral sciences.
Notes: Open to first years and sophomores in the spring; open only to first years in the fall.

TITLE: EVIL
Course Name: Evil, Distraction, and How to Build a Better World
COMMENTS: Open to First Years Only (FYC).
Course Description: When we think of evil, we often imagine Hollywood-style movie villains, people with malicious intent and genius plans to destroy the world. When we look through history, we often find that evil is much more complicated. In many cases, it is perpetrated by ordinary people who have unthinkingly adopted abhorrent views and practices accepted by their societies. The goals for this course are to ask whether we have unreflectively accepted any such views and practices, to determine what the appropriate responses to evil are once we've recognized it and to practice making the world a better place. Topics include: the nature of evil, global justice, animal suffering, treatment of the elderly, civil disobedience, and beauty standards.

TITLE: CRITICAL REASONING
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores and 1st years Not Open to Those Who Took PHIL 100W.
Course Description: This course will introduce students to both the formal study of logic and argumentation and to a wide range of creative (and ingenious!) arguments from across the history of philosophy.
Notes: Not open to students who have taken PHIL-100.

TITLE: EASTERN PHILOSOPHY
Course Description: What is the self? What is the good life for a human being? What is the relationship between humans and nature? Are all things interconnected? What is the universe fundamentally like? In this course we will explore how these questions have been addressed in Eastern philosophy, and see how life's great mysteries can be explored in a variety of ways by engaging in the numerous philosophical methods found in Eastern thought. Typical focus is on key philosophical texts from China, India, and Japan, and views often discussed include Confucianism, Daoism, Buddhism, and the various metaphysical, epistemological, and ethical aspects of different versions of these theories.

TITLE: HIST WEST PHIL (MOD)
Course Description: A survey of themes in the works of some major philosophers of the 17th and 18th centuries in Europe, taught using team-based learning.  Spurred by advances in science and criticisms of Church dogma, philosophers in the modern era attempted to reconcile the scientific revolution with a broad view of human abilities.  They constructed systematic views of the world and our place in it in order to answer big questions, including ones about appearance and reality, the relation between minds and bodies, the nature of knowledge, God, laws of nature, and free will.

TITLE: PHILOSOPHY OF SPORT
Course Description: Examining the nature and value of sport. We explore how key philosophical themes such as meaning, identity, morality, freedom, justice, and reality play out in sport. Examples of issues discussed include what sport is, and what makes an activity a sport; the connection between sport and the good life; the nature of rules and their application in sports; the identity of sports teams over time; whether players have a duty to play fair; the ethics of technological enhancement; equality of opportunity and competition; and the relationship between sport and art.

TITLE: OUR SHARED WORLD
Course Description: Most people think animals deserve some moral consideration---it would be wrong to kick your dog for no reason. But what is the nature and weight of this consideration? We will study 3 philosophical topics with the aim of answering this question. (1) What are animal minds like? Can they grieve, do they have a sense of justice, do shrimp feel pain? (2) How do we resolve inconsistencies in the ways we view animals? We eat pigs and cows, but not dogs and horses. We treat lab rats according to stringent ethical guidelines, but painfully poison them when they get in our homes. And (3) how should we relate to wild animals? Should we conserve species? Should we bring back mammoths and saber-toothed cats? Should we prevent the suffering of wild animals?

TITLE: AESTHETICS
Course Description: This course will introduce students to debates that are central to aesthetics and the philosophy of art. We will consider issues such as what makes something a work of art, why we should engage with works of art, whether beauty really is in the eye of the beholder, and what to do about works of art by morally problematic artists.

TITLE: THE BLACK SELF
Course Name: The Black Self: Identity and Consciousness
Course Description: A philosophical exploration of a variety of historical and contemporary works that illuminate and influence the phenomenological experience of being black.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy (PHIL) or Africana Studies (AFRST), or consent of instructor

TITLE: LITERARY PHILOSOPHERS
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Soph.
Course Description: What does writing style have to do with philosophical content? We will look at the "old quarrel" between the philosophers and the poets, and look at the ways in which philosophy was and is written, to think about what counts as philosophy and why and how we mark it off from its others. Readings by Borges, Calvino, Kafka, Coetzee, Plato and others.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Philosophy (PHIL), Literature (LIT), Creative Writing (CRWR) or consent of instructor

TITLE: KNOWLEDGE AND ITS LIMITS
Course Description: An advanced study of analytic epistemology. We will explore contemporary debates about the nature of knowledge, evidence, justification, the structure of the mind, and the significance of truth.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in philosophy or permission of the instructor.

TITLE: WITTGENSTEIN
Course Description: A broad study of themes through Wittgenstein’s work, including the picture-theory, naming, rule-following, meaning, skepticism, and truth.  While our focus will be on Wittgenstein’s work, we will also spend time on his intellectual forebears and those he influenced, including Frege, Russell, Anscombe, Quine, Kripke, and Diamond.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or permission of instructor
Notes: Taught in alternating years.

TITLE: PLATO
Course Description: An intensive study of the philosophical dialogues of Plato, exploring interpretive matters, historical settings, philosophical arguments, and dramatic features.  Special attention will be given to the primary texts, and some time and attention will be spent discussing secondary literature.  The course will span every major area of philosophy (including metaphysics, ethics, epistemology, aesthetics, and logic) just as the works of Plato do.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or PHIL-201

TITLE: DETACHMENT
Course Description: How much should we care about what happens in our lives? If we care too much, we risk being mired in anxiety and pain, but if we care too little, we seem to lose something central to our humanity. In this seminar we will explore how various philosophical traditions and ages, from East to West, from Ancient to Contemporary, have aimed to resolve this issue through the notion of detachment. We will consider how detachment—in its various forms—can form a central part of a good human life. We also explore critiques of detachment by examining its connections to authenticity and alienation. Examples of traditions to be explored include Stoicism, Epicureanism, Daoism, Buddhism, Existentialism, and Absurdism.
Prerequisite Narrative: Three courses in Philosophy or consent of the instructor

TITLE: SURVEY OF PHYSICS II
COMMENTS: STUDENTS WHO ENROLL ON PHYS-105 MUST ALSO ENROLL IN A PHYS-105L LAB SECTION.
Course Description: The second semester of a year-long sequence (100-105) for pre-med students and other scientists who require a year of physics. Topics include electricity, fluids, waves, optics, atomic physics and nuclear physics. Emphasis on applications of physics in medicine and in other sciences.
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory. Knowledge of algebra and trigonometry required.

TITLE: SURVEY OF PHYSICS II
Course Description: The second semester of a year-long sequence (100-105) for pre-med students and other scientists who require a year of physics. Topics include electricity, fluids, waves, optics, atomic physics and nuclear physics. Emphasis on applications of physics in medicine and in other sciences.
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory. Knowledge of algebra and trigonometry required.

TITLE: PHYSICS AND ART
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: This course is a survey of some of the interesting ways in which fine art intersects math and physics. The curriculum consists of six topics in which some juxtaposition of physics and art is present; in some cases physics is relevant to the context of the art, in some case to the content of the art, and in some cases, both. We begin with some of the earliest works of art and proceed chronologically,  including cave paintings and radiocarbon dating, the Archimedes palimpsest and imaging techniques, and the drip paintings of Jackson Pollock  and their connection to chaotic motion and fractals.
Notes: Familiarity with algebra and calculus recommended.

TITLE: WAVES AND FIELDS
COMMENTS: STUDENTS WHO ENROLL FOR PHYS 195 MUST SIGN UP FOR PHYS 195L.
Course Description: The physics of oscillations, waves and fields. Topics include simple harmonic motion, fluids, sound, electric and magnetic fields, light, optics and interference phenomena. Emphasizes the use of calculus as a tool to describe and analyze the physical world.  Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-190 or PHYS-200 and MATH-116 (may be taken concurrently)

TITLE: PHYSICS II
COMMENTS: STUDENTS WHO ENROLL FOR PHYS 205 MUST ALSO SIGN UP FOR PHYS 205L.
Course Description: The second semester of a year-long sequence (200-205) for pre-med students and other scientists who require a year of physics. Topics include electricity and magnetism, optics, relativity, atomic physics and nuclear physics.
Notes: Three hours of lecture and three hours of laboratory.

TITLE: ELECTRONICS & COMPUTERS
Course Description: Hands-on introduction to the concepts and devices of electronics. Study of analog and digital circuits, computer architecture, assembler programming and computer interfacing.
Notes: Six hours of laboratory

TITLE: ELECTROMAGNETISM
Course Description: Introduction to the mathematical description of the electric and magnetic fields, their sources and their interactions with matter. Exploration of Maxwell’s laws with emphasis on the relationship between the physics and the mathematics needed to describe it.
Notes: Normally taken concurrently with PHYS-245. MATH-216 is recommended. Three hours of class.

TITLE: TOPIC MATHEMATICAL PHYS
Course Description: A study of mathematical methods and their use in investigating physical systems. Topics may include ordinary differential equations, special functions, Sturm-Liouville theory, partial differential equations, integral transforms, calculus of complex functions, numerical methods, tensor analysis, and group theory.
Prerequisite Narrative: MATH-224 and either PHYS-295 or MATH-216, or permission of instructor
Notes: Normally offered in alternate years

TITLE: TOPICS IN QUANTUM PHYSICS
Course Description: Exploration of topics in contemporary physics using the tools of quantum mechanics developed in PHYS-290. Topics may include multi-electron atoms, molecules, solid state physics, lasers and quantum optics, nuclear physics, quantum computing, and particle physics.

TITLE: SCI, TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
COMMENTS: Restricted to CHEM and PHYS majors. 0.5 credit class; Runs from 1/20/27 to 3/12/27.
Course Description: An examination of the assumptions, paradigms, and hierarchies embedded in science and technology. This course will examine evidence pointing to the structure of hierarchies built into and from science and how those structures may result in inequalities for various groups participating in and affected by science and technology. Topics will vary but might include: the objectivity/subjectivity of science; how biases and social structures intersect with equity, diversity, and inclusion in science; and gender and race disparities in STEM fields.
Prerequisite Narrative: Restricted to Chemistry or Physics concentrators or permission of the instructor.

TITLE: PHYSICS AND SOCIETY II
COMMENTS: 0.5 credit course; Runs 3/29/27 through 5/17/27.
Course Description: A continuation of PHYS/CHEM 348, focused on applying the general material learned in PHYS/CHEM 348 to real life intersections of physics activities and broader society. In addition to an in-depth case study, students will complete projects using their knowledge of social, structural, and institutional hierarchies to improve the Physics Department.
Notes: This is a half credit continuation of PHYS/CHEM 348 into the second half of the semester.

TITLE: RESEARCH SEMINAR
Course Description: A series of research projects stressing the integration of theory and experiment. Emphasis on scientific writing, formal oral presentations, use of the current physics literature.
Usual instructor: Charles Collet; Amani Jayakody; Viva Horowitz

TITLE: ELECTROMAGNETIC THEORY
Course Description: Intensive study of Maxwell’s equations in both differential and integral form; electrostatics and electro-dynamics; special relativity; and the transformation of electromagnetic fields. Introduction to electromagnetic waves and dielectric and magnetic materials.
Prerequisite Narrative: PHYS-295 and PHYS-350 or consent of instructor

TITLE: SENIOR RESEARCH PROJECT
Course Description: Independent research in collaboration with faculty supervisor. Students will give a series of formal oral presentations about their research and will write a comprehensive thesis.
Notes: Open to senior concentrators or to others with consent of instructor.

TITLE: SENIOR RESEARCH
Course Description: Independent research in collaboration with faculty supervisor. Students will give a series of formal oral presentations about their research and will write a comprehensive thesis.

TITLE: INTRODUCTION TO LAW
Course Description: Focus on the American system of law: principally constitutional law, criminal law, and the development of civil rights. Topics include philosophical approaches to justice, English common law, and comparative analysis of French civil law and legal codes in socialist political systems and in majority Muslim countries. Consideration of the challenges to trust in legal institutions from the Supreme Court to local courts and police. Attention also to legal regimes regarding refugees, Native Americans, and defendants with mental illness.

TITLE: INTRO PUBLIC POLICY
COMMENTS: Open to Sophomore &  Junior GOVT/PPOL Majors Only.
Course Description: The study of policy analysis using and comparing a variety of disciplinary and analytic traditions.  Consideration of controversies over particular policies at the national and local level and the premises underlying them.   Examination of methods and principles used in formulating and  evaluating public policy.
Notes: Open to seniors with consent of instructor. (American Politics)

TITLE: JUSTICE LAB SEMINAR
COMMENTS: Open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
Course Description: This seminar forms part of the justice lab program. It focuses on issues of politics and policy.
Usual instructor: Heather Sullivan (and others in the gov department)
Notes: This course forms part of the Justice Lab. Students must apply to be a part of the lab.

TITLE: SENIOR PROJECT
Course Description: A one semester senior project, culminating in a public policy analysis. This is the capstone course in the Public Policy concentration.

TITLE: INTRO TO PSYCHOLOGY
COMMENTS: Not Open to Those Who Took 200-300. Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr. Students may only take one full credit 100-level PSYCH course.
Course Description: An introduction to the science of human behavior. Topics include the nervous system, perception, learning, motivation, cognitive and social development, personality, individual differences, social behavior and psychopathology. In class laboratory exercises to emphasize the use of research methods and data to describe and examine behavior.
Notes: Some sections may be offered as First-Year Courses.

TITLE: INTRO TO PSYCHOLOGY
COMMENTS: Open to First Years Only.  Not Open to Those Who Took 200-300. Students may only take one full credit 100-level PSYCH course.
Course Description: An introduction to the science of human behavior. Topics include the nervous system, perception, learning, motivation, cognitive and social development, personality, individual differences, social behavior and psychopathology. In class laboratory exercises to emphasize the use of research methods and data to describe and examine behavior.
Notes: Some sections may be offered as First-Year Courses.

TITLE: STATS & RESEARCH METHODS
Course Name: Statistics and Research Methods in Psychology
Course Description: The application and interpretation of descriptive and inferential statistics in the study of psychological processes. Some instruction in research design and methodological issues. Students will learn to use the statistical computer program SPSS to analyze data. Topics include the principles of hypothesis testing, t tests, analysis of variance, regression, and some non-parametric statistics.

TITLE: STATS & RESEARCH METHODS
Course Name: Statistics and Research Methods in Psychology
Course Description: The application and interpretation of descriptive and inferential statistics in the study of psychological processes. Some instruction in research design and methodological issues. Students will learn to use the statistical computer program SPSS to analyze data. Topics include the principles of hypothesis testing, t tests, analysis of variance, regression, and some non-parametric statistics.

TITLE: HUMAN NEUROSCIENCE
Course Description: Introduction to the field of neuroscience from a behavioral and cognitive perspective. Survey of experimental and clinical research involving humans and non-human animals, addressing presumed neural mechanisms for cognitive, motivational and emotional states. Analysis of amnesia, aphasia, agnosias, apraxias and disconnection syndromes.

TITLE: HUMAN NEUROSCIENCE
Course Description: Introduction to the field of neuroscience from a behavioral and cognitive perspective. Survey of experimental and clinical research involving humans and non-human animals, addressing presumed neural mechanisms for cognitive, motivational and emotional states. Analysis of amnesia, aphasia, agnosias, apraxias and disconnection syndromes.

TITLE: COUNSELING PSYCHOLOGY
Course Description: An overview of the theoretical orientations, treatment approaches and empirical literature in the field of counseling psychology. Examines the mechanisms by which counseling interventions facilitate personal and interpersonal functioning with a focus on emotional, social, educational, vocational and developmental concerns.
Notes: Does not count toward the Psychology or Neuroscience concentration or the Psychology minor.

TITLE: PSYCH BIAS JUSTICE SYSTEM
Course Name: Psychological Bias in the Justice System
COMMENTS: The 200-level of this course is open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
Course Description: How does group membership (e.g., sex, race, mental health status) shape one's experiences with the criminal justice system? Adopting a chronological approach through an exemplar criminal case (e.g., arrest, arraignment, plea bargaining, trial, sentencing, release), this course will use case law and empirical research to explore the law's continuing efforts - and shortcomings - in addressing and decreasing bias. Does not count toward the Psychology or Neuroscience concentration or the Psychology minor.
Notes: Not open to students who have taken PSYCH 367.

TITLE: PSYCH GENDER LEADERSHIP
Course Description: Theoretical and methodological examination of how leadership potential is socially constructed, evaluated, and rewarded, and how these processes are shaped by gender stereotypes. Topics include leadership prototypes, role congruity and lack-of-fit models, backlash and bias, intersectionality, and the effects of gender and race on leadership evaluations. Class time is devoted to in-depth analysis of research articles and case studies, along with student-led discussions and presentations. Laboratory component involves two original research projects with data collection, statistical analysis, scholarly writing, and oral presentations.
Notes: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory work.

TITLE: STRESS & PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGY
Course Description: A theoretical and methodological exploration of the psychological and physiological mechanisms of stress. Questions will include: How does psychological stress impact health and well-being? What neurobiological mechanisms are involved? What is the role of environmental context? Laboratory exercises will include designing original experiments to examine the role of stress on behavior and physiological activity, as well as analyzing data, writing papers based on findings, and oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Prerequisite Narrative: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201 and PSYCH-204 / NEURO-204 or PSYCH-205 / NEURO-205
Prerequisites: PSYCH-201, , NEURO-201, , PSYCH-204, , NEURO-204, , PSYCH-205, , NEURO-205,
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology. (Same as PSYCH-329, NEURO-329.)

TITLE: SYSTEMS NEUROSCIENCE
Course Description: The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.

TITLE: SYSTEMS NEUROSCIENCE
Course Description: The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
Notes: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.

TITLE: PSYCHOLOGY OF FRIENDSHIP
Course Description: An exploration of theoretical and empirical research on the psychology of friendship, with an emphasis on sociocultural and evolutionary approaches. We will consider questions such as: What is friendship, and what functions does it serve in our lives? How do we seek and maintain friendships? In what ways is friendship similar and different across cultures? Through activities and reflections, students will use course material as a lens for examining their own important relationships.

TITLE: ADULT PSYCHOPATHOLOGY
Course Description: Introduction to the study of mental disorders in adults, including historical and cultural perspectives. Focus on classification, diagnostic assessment, etiology, treatment, and evaluation of treatment efficacy for the major disorders including anxiety, affective, thought, substance, and eating disorders. Research methods in clinical psychology emphasized. Discussion will include how gender, race, ethnicity, culture, sexuality, and social class relate to our understanding of mental illness and its treatment.

TITLE: PSYCH BIAS JUSTICE SYSTEM
Course Name: Psychological Bias in the Justice System
Course Description: How does group membership (e.g., sex, race, ethnicity, religion) shape one’s experiences with the criminal justice system? Adopting a chronological approach through an exemplar criminal case (e.g., arrest, arraignment, plea bargaining, trial, sentencing, release), this course will use case law and empirical research to explore the law’s continuing efforts—and shortcomings—in addressing and decreasing bias.
Notes: Not open to students who have taken PSYCH 267.

TITLE: LIFESPAN DEVELOPMENT
Course Description: An introduction to the science of lifespan development, from conception and prenatal development to older age and death. Focuses on multiple domains of development, including cognitive, social, physical, and emotional, with emphasis on how development in all domains is shaped by both biological and social/cultural influences (e.g., gender norms, social class, stereotyping and prejudice).

TITLE: ANCIENT JEWISH WISDOM
Course Description: An introduction to the Jewish Tradition and Jewish way of reading.

TITLE: RELIGION AND ECOLOGY
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: This course explores ‘Religion and Ecology,’ beginning from a North American starting point in the 1960s amidst a budding environmentalist movement. Readings explore how mainly Christian theological communities engaged with a new social movement, before broadening to other religious traditions. The course then proceeds via a new theoretical frame: the religious lives of human communities are located within deep time and geographical space, with an eye to the migration history of the human as a natural kind. Along the way, we responsibly speculate about communities located in (what is now) Africa, the Middle East, Europe, Asia, and the Americas. The course ends by asking: how are we to live into a shared environmental future, and what is the role of our deepest religious commitments?

TITLE: SACRED IN SOUTH ASIA
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Years, Sophomores, & Juniors.
Course Description: What constitutes the sacred in south Asia? Is it a person, place, river, hill, temple or nature/ecology? Where and how did the notion of sacrality emerge in South Asia? Is it linked exclusively to religious institutions or is it found in the daily lives of people? This course will examine these questions by exploring the multiple religious traditions of South Asia and examining their essential beliefs, doctrines, institutions, rituals and popular practices through a study of texts, material culture, films and ethnographic accounts.

TITLE: WORLD FILMS, WORLD FAITHS
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Sophomores, & Juniors.
Course Description: Introduces the practices and beliefs of several major world religions (including Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism) through the medium of film. Exploring Japanese anime, Indonesia documentaries, video films from Ghana, Bollywood mythologicals, Jesus-films from Latin America, Korean-Buddhist films, contemporary fictional glimpses into Jewish life, and more, shows how religious people live and struggle and find joy, by using the audio-visual medium of film.
Notes: Evening film screenings.

TITLE: MEDIEVAL CHRISTIANITIES
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Sophomores, & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: A survey of the development of the Christian religion in premodern Eurasia and the Mediterranean, from its elevation to a state cult in the later Roman Empire to about 1450. Special consideration will be given to the growth of the church and processes of conversion, the problem of authority versus heresy and heterodoxy, and the relationship of the Christian churches to Islam and other non-Christian peoples. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.
Notes: Open to First and Second Year Students Only.

TITLE: READINGS IN RELIGIOUS STUDIES
COMMENTS: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Years.
Course Description: Religious Studies faculty join with students to read and discuss one important and/or provocative work each semester.
Notes: Students may take this course as many times as desired.

TITLE: SOCIAL LIVES ANCIENT DEAD
Course Name: The Social Lives of the Ancient Dead
Course Description: What happened to people after they died in the ancient world? Often, their story was only beginning. This course looks at the ways the dead remained part of everyday life. We will read curse tablets that call on restless spirits, laws about stolen bodies, stories about cities fighting over heroic bones, and Christian accounts of remains that heal or protect the living. We will also study tombs and inscriptions to see how people used the dead to make claims about family, memory, status, and belonging. The course ends close to home. For the final project, students will turn to Hamilton’s own cemetery and investigate how one grave, monument, or burial story creates a social life for the dead on our campus. The larger question throughout the course is simple: what can the dead still do for the living?
Notes: (Application, Interpretation)

TITLE: MINORITIES IN THE MIDDLE EAST
Course Name: Minorities in the Middle East: History, Religion, and Relations with Political Powers
Course Description: This course explores how minority communities in the Middle East—Druze, ʿAlawites, Kurds, Yezidis, Armenians, Maronites, Copts, Assyrians, and others—have been formed and transformed from the late Ottoman era to the present. Beginning with the shift from imperial pluralism to nation-state “minorities,” it examines how religion, identity, nationalism, and political power shape communal identity and minority–state relations. Case studies span Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, addressing genocide, displacement, nationalism, citizenship, security, and diaspora. Drawing on history, anthropology, religious studies, and political science, students examine how communities negotiate identity, power, and recognition in a plural Middle East. This course examines historical and contemporary experiences of minority communities in the Middle East. Some course materials address difficult subjects, including genocide, mass violence, persecution, forced displacement, sexual violence, religious and ethnic discrimination, and war. These topics are approached in their historical and scholarly contexts and are essential to understanding the experiences of the communities studied in the course.

TITLE: JEWISH FEMINISM
Course Description: This course examines the foundational texts, debates, and activism of Jewish feminism in the United States from the early 1970s to the present. Students will explore how Jewish women named and theorized gender inequality in Jewish law, ritual, theology, communal life, and cultural practice—and how those critiques reshaped American Judaism. Readings will situate Jewish feminist thought within wider developments in feminist, religious, and American social history. The course also considers LGBTQ Jewish ideas and activism, asking where they converge with, extend, or challenge Jewish feminist concerns. Students will gain a vocabulary for analyzing the movement’s central questions, historical evolution, and enduring impact on Jewish life today.

TITLE: AMERICAN JEWISH LITERATURE
Course Description: What makes a work “Jewish American literature”? Must it be written by a Jewish author, center Jewish characters or themes, or appear in a Jewish language? This course uses such questions to explore the American Jewish experience from the earliest Jewish settlement to the present, with particular attention to the period after 1865. Through fiction, poetry, memoir, drama, and other genres, students will examine how writers have represented migration, religion, family, race, belonging, assimilation, and cultural difference. Rather than imposing fixed definitions, the course treats “Jewish,” “American,” and “literature” as contested categories whose meanings have changed over time.

TITLE: CONSPIRACY THEORIES & RELIG
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: Apocalyptic visions, prophecies, and experiences of revelation have mobilized, challenged, and sustained the commitment of religious believers and conspiracy theorists alike. But what else do conspiracy theories and religions share in common, and how do they differ? This course explores intersections of religion and conspiracy theories in American culture from the 19th century to the present day. We examine historical materials alongside contemporary analyses, including millennialist tracts and sermons, conspiracy theory message board websites, illustrations of biblical prophecies, and pictograms of apocalyptic visions. Along the way, we consider how categorizations of “conspiracy theories” and “fringe” movements have served as critical sites for theorizing and delimiting the margins of “real” religion and acceptable belief.

TITLE: BUDDHIST ENVIRONMENTALISM
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: This course explores the conjunction of Buddhism and environmentalism. Part I considers advocates of this combination, or “eco-Buddhists,” with a focus on those who criticize current structures of political economy. Classical texts from the Buddhist canon (Nagarjuna, the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Lotus Sutra, etc.) will be introduced with an eye to seeing where eco-Buddhists derive some of their core claims. Part II considers critics of eco-Buddhists, who raise the objection that historical Buddhists never held commitments like those of modern-day environmentalists. Could eco-Buddhism even be a new form of Orientalism? The course concludes by making sense of these critiques on the way to a historically responsible description of what a modern Buddhist environmentalism might be.
Notes: (Location)

TITLE: MOTHER NATURE
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: How have people in India understood and interacted with mother nature? How do they conceptualize the environment and ecosystems? How do they deal with climate change and ecological disasters? What role does religion play in shaping human attitude to the mother nature? Focusing on Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, the course examines how Indian communities have engaged and negotiated their relationships with the natural world to consider themes including the conception of environment as sacred space, ethical living, non-violence, animal-protection, and food-culture.
Notes: No prior coursework on Religion or Asia is required.

TITLE: IMAGINING RELIGIONS
COMMENTS: Open to Seniors, Juniors, & Sophomores.
Course Description: Students will learn to imagine, analyze, and interpret religion(s) in a wide variety of ways. Students will engage critically with the category of "religion" and related concepts such as sacred space, the other, colonialism, modernity, globalization, and comparison.

TITLE: RELIGION AND MAGIC
Course Description: Hypnotism. Stage magic. Wonder shows. What do these things have to do with religion? This course explores this question as we trace various intersections of magic and religion from the 18th century to the present day, examining topics including occult and esoteric movements, conjuring practices, mesmerism, hypnotism, spiritualism, telepathy, and stage magic performances. Throughout this course, we engage with critical theories and methods in the study of religion that shed light on the religious dimensions of magic and magical dynamics of religion. In addition to scholarly works from the fields of religious studies and cultural history, we examine a range of cultural data and historical artifacts, from colonial-era trials against alleged sorcerers to 20 th century scientific experiments in psychic phenomena.

TITLE: HOW SATAN BECAME THE DEVIL
Course Description: Satan does not enter history as the horned ruler of hell we recognize today. This course follows how a relatively minor figure in early Jewish traditions became Christianity’s great enemy of God. Along the way, we will meet fallen angels who teach humans forbidden knowledge, demons who possess bodies, monks who claim to wrestle with the Devil in the desert, and exorcists trying to identify what has taken control of a person. We will also see how Satan became connected to heresy, witchcraft, and fears about the end of the world. Rather than treating the Devil as one unchanging character, we will ask why different societies kept reinventing him. Students will explore a larger question: what does a culture reveal about itself when it decides what evil looks like?
Notes: (Application, Interpretation)

TITLE: MODERN RUSSIAN HISTORY
Course Description: An overview of Russian history from the emancipation of the serfs to the collapse of the Soviet Union. Themes of the course include how Russia and the USSR dealt with their sense of "backwardness" compared to Europe, the multi-national and multi-religious nature of this vast Eurasian state, and the meanings of "modernity."

TITLE: LIT & REV:20TH & 21ST CENTURY
Course Name: Literature and Revolution: Twentieth- and Twenty-First Century Russian and Soviet Fiction.
Course Description: This course offers a survey of twentieth- and twenty-first-century Russian and Soviet fiction, focusing on the literature that defined this transformative period in Russia’s modern history.
Notes: Taught in English. No knowledge of Russian required.

TITLE: RUSSIA AND THE WORLD
Course Description: The course will examine Russia’s relations with both its post-Soviet neighbors and the West from the Tsarist era to the present. Topics to be covered include: the formation of the Russian Empire, the Cold War, the evolution of Russian-Western relations since the collapse of communism, Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, and the outbreak of a major war with Ukraine in 2022. A central theme of the course will be the evolution of Russian national identity, especially as it relates to Russia’s status as an empire and its relationship with the West.
Prerequisite Narrative: Take any one of the following: GOVT-112, GOVT-114, one Russian Studies course, or consent of instructor.
Notes: (International Relations)

TITLE: SIBERIAN TEXT
Course Description: This course is an exploration of five centuries of writing in and about Siberia. While we will root ourselves in the socio-historical context, our main goal is to engage meaningfully with the very process of the formation of the Siberian Text. By this, scholars of the region mean the body of works that emerged out of the geographical, political, anthropological, and cultural categorizations of Siberia. The plurality of voices and the diversity of spatial experiences engaged in the process of creating the Siberian Text include travelers, criminals, political prisoners, religious dissenters, shamans, hunters, ethnographers, missionaries, vagabonds, and peasants. Probing the fraught legacy of the current spatial discourse on Siberia, the course will examine a variety of media and genres, including official documents, travelogues, oral tradition(s), works of fiction, autobiographies, pictorial art, and film. In addition to the transnational and transhistorical dimensions, we will engage with theories of space and place, imagined geographies, and ecocriticism.
Notes: Taught in English.

TITLE: SECOND TERM RUSSIAN
Course Description: Continued development of skills in spoken and written Russian. Intensive use of audio/visual and computer materials.

TITLE: FOURTH TERM RUSSIAN
Course Description: Continuation of third-term Russian. Introduction to the language of popular culture, including contemporary film and music.

TITLE: ADVANCED RUSSIAN II
Course Description: Continuation of Russian Studies 370. The focus of this class will be on writing, reading, and talking about daily life, or "byt" in diary form, broadly conceived. Works of literature and culture will be compared with social media posts in both long (blog posts) and short formats (memes, tweets, tik toks, etc). Advanced readings and discussion will be accompanied by a thorough review of grammar and difficult grammar points.

TITLE: INTRODUCTORY SOCIOLOGY
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores Only Not Open to Those Who Took Soc 110.
Course Description: Sociological perspective on human behavior. Classic and contemporary sociological concepts that further an understanding of the structure, process, stability and change of social life.
Notes: Not open to students who have taken SOC-110.

TITLE: SOC HEALTH & ILLNESS
Course Name: The Sociology of Health and Illness
Course Description: This course will give students an introduction to the sociological study of health and illness. While sociologists have taken the study of medicine seriously since at least the 1950s, health and illness are phenomena whose relationship to human society and experience are long and complex. In order to explore this reality, this class will draw on the empirical work of historians, anthropologists, sociologists, and even fiction writers to explore the personal and social elements of sickness and health.

TITLE: SOCIOLOGY OF ELITES
Course Description: Who rules—and how do they stay on top? This course examines inequality from above, exploring how elites are formed, legitimated, and challenged across diverse settings. Case studies range from Ivy League admissions and Wall Street hiring to technology elites, Russian oligarchs, emergent Chinese elites, Indian caste hierarchies, and royal families in the Gulf. We will explore how class, race, and gender shape the formation of elite groups, their capacity to appropriate resources, and their struggles with rival elites over power and resources. By the end of the course, students will have the analytical tools to understand not just who holds power, but how that power is reproduced, justified, and contested.
Notes: Retakeable up to two times.

TITLE: SOCIOLOGY OF EDUCATION
Course Description: This course provides a sociological lens for analyzing education and educational inequality in the United States. Over the course of the semester, we will use various theories to explore education as a social institution, going beyond our own individual experiences and personal ideologies. In addition to covering the foundational ideas in the sociology of education, we will spend considerable time exploring the myriad ways that education impacts, and is impacted by, broader patterns of inequality. We will also use empirical studies to examine external factors that affect student experiences and shape learning outcomes; factors such as the role of families, neighborhoods, and schools, themselves. Salient topics include racial segregation, economic stratification within and between schools, technology, tracking, teacher pedagogy, immigration, English Language Learners, punishment, higher education, and the future of education in a demographically and culturally diversifying society.

TITLE: CRIME, LAW, AND INEQUALITY
Course Description: This course examines crime, criminalization, and social control from a sociological perspective. Rather than treating crime as simply the violation of law, we examine how crime is socially and politically constructed and how practices of punishment and regulation emerge through broader struggles over power, morality, and social order. Topics include moral panics, addiction and criminalization, policing and surveillance, mass incarceration, organized crime, mafia networks, illicit drug economies, corporate crime, state violence, terrorism, and border enforcement. Students will critically evaluate competing explanations of crime and examine how criminalization and social control both shape and are shaped by relations of power, inequality, governance, and social change.

TITLE: WORK, ORGANIZATIONS & INEQUAL
Course Description: This course will examine how complex organizations structure work in the United States, how work has changed, and why. We will examine the structure of work from an organizational perspective, which introduces students to a framework for thinking about how social institutions (such as federal policies or racial inequality) shape the experiences of the everyday people. Students will begin to deepen their knowledge about the structure of work in the U.S., why it looks the way that it does today, and who benefits (or does not benefit) from this system.

TITLE: SOCIOLOGY OF IMMIGRATION
Course Description: This course examines international migration as a social process, with a main focus on immigration to the United States. It provides sociological perspectives to understand why immigration happens, how it occurs, and what consequences and outcomes it produces. We will explore theories of migration and compare and contrast trends in old world and new world migration systems, as well as the American migration experience.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Sociology (SOC) or consent of instructor

TITLE: GLOBAL COMMEMORATION
Course Description: This course examines how atrocities - big and small - are remembered around the globe: What is the process through which individual experiences are transformed into credible testimonies and collective traumas? What role do state actors, educational institutions, community organizations, and civic society play in the production of memory? And what is the purpose of keeping the past alive if societies are ever-changing and evolving? We will trace the long-lasting legacies of human brutality to different parts of the globe. By listening to survivors, exploring different forms of testimonies, and combing through evidence accumulated by investigative journalists, we will critically engage with and expand upon foundational sociological texts on history, memory, and commemoration.

TITLE: SOCIOLOGICAL THEORY
Course Description: Examination of classic and contemporary sociological concepts and perspectives. The theorists covered include Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Freud, Mead, Berger and Luckmann, and Foucault.

TITLE: URBAN AMERICA
Course Description: Although globalization scholars at the turn of the millennium predicted the loss of importance of the local, cities have continued to be vital anchors of social, economic, political, and cultural life. While they may serve as a safe haven for some, they are simultaneously the site of continuous political struggles over the boundaries of belonging. Tracing the history of urbanization in the U.S., this course explores various facets of contemporary urban life, including urban disempowerment, poverty, segregation, and gentrification. At the same time, we will look at the many ways in which residents – including migrants and members of the LGBTQIA+ community – claim their right to the city.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Sociology (SOC) or consent of instructor

TITLE: SOCIOLOGY OF VIOLENCE
Course Description: Violence is deeply intertwined with power, inequality, and struggles among social groups, political movements, and the state. It ranges from direct physical harm to structural and symbolic forms that often go unrecognized as violence at all. This course traces how power inequalities enable violence and its erasure, and how state and nonstate violence interact to reproduce or reshape those inequalities. Using a comparative global approach, we examine specific sites and collective contentious events where these dynamics become visible, from prisons and borders to war and militarized conflict, genocide, torture, counterinsurgency, terrorism, and counterrevolution.
Prerequisite Narrative: Students must have taken SOC-101, SOC-110, or SOC-126

TITLE: MEDICINE IN AMERICA
Course Description: We take for granted medicine as we know it today, yet at the turn of the 20th century, medical practice could have taken any number of directions. Why did allopathic medicine win out over its competitors to consolidate professional and cultural authority over health? How has the patient-provider relationship evolved from an asymmetric model to one characterized by patient consumerism? How do trainees learn medicine’s “hidden curriculum”? Looking forward, how will providers fare against challenges to autonomy posed by insurance companies, for-profit hospitals, politicians, and AI? To answer these and related questions, this course draws on empirical studies, historical accounts, and media to examine how the profession of medicine has been constructed, contested, and transformed over time.

TITLE: SEM SOC PRODUCTION FOOD
Course Name: Seminar on the Social Production of Food
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., and Sophomores.
Course Description: Examines the production and consumption of food in contemporary societies from a sociological perspective. We will study how food shapes personal identity and communal life; the organizational and institutional contexts food production from farm to table; the role food plays in popular culture and the rise of alternative food movements. Covers such topics as food, communal identity and family; the culture and practices of "Foodies"; the world of the restaurant kitchen; globalization and changes in farming and food consumption.

TITLE: SOCIOLOGY OF CLIMATE ACTION
Course Name: Sociology of Climate Change and Climate Action
Course Description: In the face of the ongoing climate crisis, we are also witnessing deployment of climate solutions: electrification of transportation, renewable energy development, reforestation initiatives, and reductions in animal agriculture. How do communities react to these approaches to climate action? We unpack theoretical and on-the-ground perspectives on what climate change means among different groups of people and explore people’s social location influences how they understand and respond to it individually and collectively. We examine how colonialism, and macroeconomic structures shape perspectives on the experience of the climate crisis and responses to it. Students apply their theoretical understanding in structured community conversations about climate solutions with community stakeholders.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Environmental Studies or Sociology

TITLE: AI AND SOCIETY
Course Description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) will shape society in profound ways, disrupting fields like higher education, government, science, or medicine. Yet integrating AI responsibly into society remains difficult. This course explores the sociological dimensions of AI, from its historical roots to today's debates around bias, autonomy, and changing human relationships. Students will critically examine how AI systems perceive, reason, and communicate, with emphasis on machine learning's role in driving AI capabilities. The course also unpacks the politics of algorithms, data, and code, and how AI is socially shaped in practice. Drawing on social science research on technology, work, media, and inequalities, students will investigate how AI can be developed and deployed in ways that align with human values and create meaningful social impact.

TITLE: INTRO TO MAKING THETR
Course Name: "Playing" Introduction to Making Theatre: Theory and Practice
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: This is the gateway course for all theatre courses. This class combines the study of theatre and drama as it reflects, represents and interprets diverse cultures with a hands-on examination of how theatre is made.  Through readings, lectures, discussions and projects the class will explore the ideas, strategies and languages of theatre (acting, directing, playwriting, designing) that theatre artists use to create contemporary theatrical performance.
Notes: One section for first-year students only; first-years and sophomores. Juniors with permission of the Department.

TITLE: ACTING STYLES: REALISM
Course Description: Acting workshop is a critical level acting course that teaches students how to make strong acting choices by learning what questions to ask.

TITLE: PRODUCTION
COMMENTS: Instructor's Signature Req.
Course Description: The study of theatre through participation (performance, management and/or technical work) in a faculty-directed production. Students must pre-register for this class; for 141F first-year students may register during orientation. Preregistration does not guarantee an acting role.  Auditions will take place at the start of the semester, and students not acting will perform a technical/production role.
Notes: One-half credit. May be repeated for credit.

TITLE: STAGE COMBAT
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: This is a class on stage combat, armed and unarmed. How to safely fight on stage and make it look real.

TITLE: LIGHTING DESIGN
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: An in-depth exploration of lighting and projection design for live performance.  The course will cover the process, techniques, equipment and methodologies of these theatre design disciplines.  These include; composition, color theory, projection mapping, CAD drafting, as well as lighting for the camera.

TITLE: SCENE PAINTING
COMMENTS: Open to Seniors, Juniors, and Sophomores.
Course Description: Through a series of projects and demonstrations, introduces students to the basic principles of scenic painting for film, television and the performing arts. Topics covered will include color mixing, texture,faux finishing (wood grain, marble, etc.), brush and spray techniques, trompe-l’oeil and large scale cartooning andpainting.
Prerequisite Narrative: THETR-105, THETR-130, or a 100-level Art course

TITLE: STAGE MANAGEMENT
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr.
Course Description: Through this course students will learn the principles of stage management for theatrical productions. How to facilitate the needs of the production through each of its stages, create industry-standard procedures, paperwork, develop good communication/organizational skills as well as an appreciation of the tact/details that stage managers bring to each production.

TITLE: INTERMED MEDIA: NEW FRONTIERS
Course Name: Intermediate Media: New Frontiers in Storytelling
COMMENTS: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab.
Course Description: This class will survey and create emergent and non -linear forms of storytelling using digital and hybrid tools. We will examine notions of narrative authority and hybridity in a digital age and think through different ways we might use technology to distill, break apart or reify modes of communication and visual metaphor. Discussion will push boundaries of traditional storytelling and consider connectivity, liveness and embodied presence. This course will draw on multiple forms of expression including but not limited to digital media, performance, sound, XR, web, and network environments.
Prerequisite Narrative: Any intro-level Digital Arts studio course, including cross-listed.
Prerequisites: ART-113, , DARTS-113, , MUSIC-113, , ART 116, , DARTS-212, , ART-213, , DARTS-213, , ART-221, , DARTS-221, , MUSIC-270,

TITLE: ADV ACTING:SHAKESPEARE
Course Name: Advanced Acting Workshop: Shakespeare and Company
Course Description: Classical texts and contemporary performance. Focus on Shakespeare, language and character. May include other classical dramatists Scene and monologue work, textual analysis, vocal and speaking preparedness, verse and heightened speech, characterization, improvisation and rehearsals.
Prerequisite Narrative: THETR-102 and THETR-201 or consent of instructor

TITLE: INTRO WOMEN&GENDER STUDIES
Course Name: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies
COMMENTS: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only. This section is Speaking Intensive.
Course Description: An interdisciplinary investigation of past and present views of women and their roles, treatment and experiences in institutions such as the family, the state, the work force, language and sexuality. The diversity of women’s experiences across age, class, ethnic, sexual, racial and national lines introduced, and theories of feminism and of women’s studies discussed.
Notes: May be offered as a standard course or FYC as well as writing intensive, non-writing intensive, or speaking intensive at the discretion of the department. Please check the schedule for details.

TITLE: BLACK WOMEN'S LIT RENAISSANCE
COMMENTS: Open to First Years and Sophomores only.
Course Description: The twenty-year period between 1970 and 1990 is often referred to as the “Black Women’s Literary Renaissance” due to the unprecedented amount of literary and cultural production from black women in the United States. This course explores its profound contributions to black life and literature. Students will examine the intersections and oppositions among political movements, such as the Lesbian Feminist Movement and the Black Power Movement, and identify how these connections shaped the aesthetic landscape of the time. Course materials will include essays, novels, poems, and visual art, featuring Alice Walker, Toni Cade Bambara, bell hooks, Lorna Simpson, and others.

TITLE: INTRO FEMINIST THOUGHT
Course Description: An interdisciplinary examination of the history and contemporary practice of feminist thought. Topics include the history of feminist thought in Western culture, the broadening and complication of that canon to include examinations of race, class, gender, sexuality, ableism and ageism, and the implications of global feminist thought.
Notes: (Political Theory)

TITLE: WOMEN AND WAR
Course Name: Women and War: Feminism, Militarism, and Nationalism
Course Description: This course examines the ways war and processes of militarization impact women in the Global North and the Global South.  Discussion will be accompanied by an analysis of categories such as “women,” “gender” and “sexuality” in relation to the “state” and “nation” during periods of warfare and armed conflict. We will engage with a range of interdisciplinary texts on gender and militarism.  These narratives will be grounded by theoretical readings that explore the ongoing debates and tensions among feminists regarding nationalism, violence, war and militarization.
Prerequisite Narrative: WMGST-101 or consent of the instructor.

TITLE: GENDER,SPACE,IDENTITY
Course Name: Gender, Space and Identity in the African Diaspora
COMMENTS: Open to Srs., Jrs., Sophomores, & 1st Yrs.
Course Description: This course examines how racialized and gendered identities are made in relation to space. How does gender intersect with race, class and other power relations embedded in the places we live? How do women and men come to occupy different places in the world – literally and figuratively – or occupy the same places in different ways? Case studies focus on identity making in relation to the body and the course more broadly focuses on the intersection of race, class, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity as matrices of social and structural power relations and hierarchies.

TITLE: SEMINAR ON AGING
Course Description: Focuses on experiences of aging with attention to midlife and beyond. Examines images of aging in literature, film and media; ageism and its interconnections with race, class, sexual and gender identity; the relationships of aging to experiences of the body, health, economic issues, social and familial relationships; and death and dying. Considers how changing age distributions in the United States influence intergenerational relationships and social policy.
Prerequisite Narrative: One course in Women’s and Gender Studies (WMGST) or consent of instructor

TITLE: QUEER/TRANS CULTURAL PRODUC
Course Description: This course explores queer and trans cultural production, ranging from zines, film, novels, photography, television, short fiction, painting, fanfiction, installation, poetry, performance art, music, video games, and more. On one level, it offers an interdisciplinary investigation of queer and trans representation, and both the possibilities and limitations of positive images and mainstream LGBTQ visibility. On another level, we explore the ways that writers, filmmakers, and artists find meaning through LGBTQ cultural production and artistic practices. We will also consider the politics of publication and distribution. The course takes up an intersectional approach, thinking about how LGBTQ cultural production is shaped by gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, class, and ability.
Prerequisite Narrative: A course in Women's and Gender Studies or Cinema Media Studies or consent of instructor

TITLE: SEM BLACK FEMINIST THOUGHT
Course Description: Interdisciplinary examination of the tradition of black feminist thought as it spans African and African-American heritages. Exploration of how black women are not simply victims of oppression but visionary agents of change. Areas examined include history, literature,music,art,education, sociology and film. There is intersectional analysis of the social, structural, and institutional hierarchies within the identities of women of African descent (gender/transgender, race, white supremacy, sexual/affectional orientation, class, color, and ability).
